articles.title: Why JNU’s protest culture is facing quiet moment
articles.summary: JNU’s response to May sexual harassment complaints by 11 students has been muted, amid stricter protest penalties, semester break, and ICC confidentiality rules.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Protests at Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU), including the one over the Nirbhaya incident in 2012 and against a professor accused of sexual harassment in 2018, have traditionally brought classes to a standstill, kept senior administrators confined to their offices and dominated national headlines for days.Against that record, the response of the JNU campus to allegations of sexual harassment made by 11 students this May appears “markedly subdued.” The students approached JNU’s Internal Complaints Committee (ICC), alleging inappropriate conduct, sexually suggestive remarks and, according to reports, offers of higher marks in return for sexual favours. The professor has denied the allegations, which remain under inquiry.Even after classes resumed mid-July, the complaints did not immediately lead to sustained protests. Wider public attention came months later. The accused’s identity has remained outside mainstream reporting. Section 16 of Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act restricts publication of the identities of the complainant, respondent and witnesses during ICC proceedings.The clearer contrast, therefore, lies not in the absence of a name but in the limited mobilisation around the complaints. There have been no prolonged class boycotts, large cross-campus marches, demonstrations outside police stations or weeks of posters, pamphlets and general body meetings comparable to earlier campaigns.Women’s safety has previously generated such responses at JNU. After the Dec 16, 2012, Nirbhaya incident, students demonstrated at Vasant Vihar police station and Munirka before joining protests in central Delhi. The mobilisation continued through campus meetings on sexual violence, women’s freedom and policing.In 2014, students struck work against the promotion of a professor while an inquiry into sexual harassment against him was pending. JNU’s decision to replace the elected Gender Sensitisation Committee Against Sexual Harassment with a statutory ICC in 2017 also triggered resistance.A year later, allegations by eight women against a professor became a campus-wide cause. Students demonstrated outside Vasant Kunj police station. A subsequent march involving more than 1,000 students and teachers towards Parliament Street encountered barricades, water cannons and police action.JNU’s capacity for prolonged agitation has extended beyond gender issues. A Nestlé outlet near Tapti Hostel became a major political dispute in 2004 over the “corporatisation” of campus space. In 2009, electricity meters, eateries and an increase in the prospectus price from Rs 120 to Rs 200 sparked strikes and marches.The disappearance of Najeeb Ahmed, a student, in Oct 2016 led to weeks of demonstrations. At one point, protesters confined the vice-chancellor and other officials inside the administrative building. The 2019 hostel-fee agitation continued for weeks, disrupted a convocation and brought HRD ministry into negotiations.This Feb, the rustication of all four JNUSU office-bearers over an earlier stir against facial-recognition gates prompted a university-wide strike.However, rules introduced since 2023 have increased the possible penalties for protests, while the complaints this May seemed to lose momentum as they were followed by a semester break. Confidentiality around an ICC inquiry may also have limited public discussion. articles.title: Putin's Brics visit: Su-57, Super Sukhois fighter jets, S-500 on Russia’s defence offer list
articles.summary: Defence News: NEW DELHI: With Russian President Vladimir Putin landing in New Delhi on Friday, Moscow has come up with a list of defence proposals for India, includ.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: With Russian President Vladimir Putin landing in New Delhi on Friday, Moscow has come up with a list of defence proposals for India, including joint production of Su-57 fifth-generation fighter jets and over $11-billion upgrade of the Su-30MKI fleet into “Super Sukhois”. In Friday’s talks with Putin, PM Modi said that besides discussions on various topics like trade, infrastructure, energy, technology, there were talks about defence too.During Putin’s three-day stay, Russia is going to have wide-ranging defence talks about these defence proposals. Besides Su-57 jet and Su-30MKI upgrade offers, the Russian side is expected to “push for proposals for additional S-400 air-defence systems, Pantsir-S1M point-defence system, radars and strategic submarines”, defence sources told TOI. Russia has also been pushing India to consider its S-500 air-defence system, an upgraded version which can target missiles across a range of 600 km as compared to S-400's 400-km limit. For S400, Russia is offering to establish a maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) facility in India, potentially in partnership with an Indian company.With only three countries ,— US, Russia and China — in the world possessing the 5th-generation stealth fighter jet technology, “Su-57 jet is a ‘natural choice’ for India,” state-owned Russian news agency Sputnik’s India chapter said on Friday. As India had conveyed its disinterest in acquiring Lockheed Martin F-35 stealth fighter jets from the US, the only option left for India is Su-57 jets as India’s own AMCA project will take a long time and the first maiden flight of AMCA is not expected before 2029-30. With India’s fighter squadrons down to an alarming level of 29 and AMCA still a distant dream, India has been considering Su-57 jets but wants a better package from Russia with a complete transfer of technology, missile package and make-in-India offer.India is also discussing a massive upgrade for its nearly 260 Su-30MKI fighters, starting with an initial batch of 84 jets. The $11 billion “Super Sukhoi” programme involves new AESA radars, modern avionics, enhanced electronic-warfare capabilities and new engines. Reports also indicate that India plans to acquire roughly 300 R-37M missiles from Russia via direct purchase or future domestic manufacturing arrangements.

articles.title: Gurgaon waterlogging has direct bearing on human rights: HHRC
articles.summary: HHRC says recurring Gurgaon waterlogging impacts human rights; orders city-wide drainage audit, GIS mapping and revamp plan, with IIT/NIT assessment and safety steps.
articles.body: GURGAON: Recurring waterlogging in Gurgaon is not merely a civic inconvenience but has a direct bearing on citizens’ human rights, Haryana Human Rights Commission (HHRC) has observed. Taking suo motu cognisance of TOI reports, the commission ordered govt agencies to conduct a comprehensive audit of the city’s drainage and civic infrastructure.In an order published Friday, the commission noted that the problem appeared to have persisted over several years and, therefore, could not be attributed to one wet spell. Such repeated disruption of roads, schools, emergency services, water supply and everyday mobility during heavy rain could not be treated as an “unavoidable feature of urban life”, it said.Drainage was a “basic and essential prerequisite” of planned urban development, HHRC said, linking its failure with Article 21 of Constitution, which guarantees the right to life and personal liberty, including living with dignity in conditions conducive to health and safety. It also referred to the constitutional obligations related to public health and environmental protection.The HHRC full bench, comprising Justice (retd) Lalit Batra, judicial member Kuldeep Jain and member Deep Bhatia, stopped short of holding any agency responsible at this stage. It said persistent failure of essential civic infrastructure, “if attributable to neglect, inadequate planning, failure of maintenance or failure to take reasonable preventive measures”, may have a direct bearing on human rights. The proceedings, it said, would ascertain the facts, determine responsibility, and secure preventive and remedial measures.The commission pointed to the ordeal of school students stranded in buses, parents wading through flooded roads, and the difficulties in getting information about children’s safety. It also referred to reports of commuters taking disproportionately long to cover short distances and the disruption to ambulances and essential services during the Aug 24 downpour, reported by TOI.The panel stressed that Gurgaon’s civic infrastructure must match the scale and density of its population and economic activity.The commission ordered GMDA, the municipal corporation, Haryana Shehri Vikas Pradhikaran, PWD, the public health engineering department, the irrigation and water resources department, DHBVN, town planning authorities and the district administration to conduct a technical audit of Gurgaon’s drainage and associated infrastructure.The audit will have to identify the capacity of the existing storm-water network, natural drains and watercourses, chronic waterlogging points (including the 99 locations flagged by authorities), causes of water accumulation, condition of drains and pumping stations, possible interconnection of sewage and storm-water systems, vulnerable underground utilities, and road-level and drainage deficiencies.HHRC further ordered GIS-based mapping of natural and engineered drainage channels and identification of encroachments or obstructions affecting natural drainage. It asked the authorities concerned to assess whether the existing system could cope with present and projected rainfall and future urbanisation.Separately, the commission sought a report on implementation of the SOP on school transport. It called for real-time tracking of school buses; communication between schools, parents, police and the administration; designated safe holding points, and restrictions on school buses entering identified high-risk waterlogging locations during extreme rainfall.It also directed authorities to identify emergency corridors for ambulances, fire services and police, and ordered a vulnerability assessment of roads, culverts, underpasses and underground utilities, particularly around the cave-in reported near IFFCO Chowk.Agencies will have to provide details of drainage deficiencies reported during the last five years, remedial measures sanctioned and the status of their implementation. They must also furnish details of pre-monsoon desilting, pumping capacity, deployment during the Aug 24 rainfall, response times, and the time taken to clear waterlogging at major locations.The commission suggested an independent technical assessment be undertaken by an IIT, NIT or another reputable hydrological/urban infrastructure institution, covering the whole Gurgaon drainage basin rather than examining individual waterlogging spots in isolation.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Gurgaon | Silver Rate in Gurgaon | Bank Holidays in Gurgaon | Public Holidays in Gurgaon | Gurgaon AQI | Weather in Gurgaon | Petrol Price in Gurgaon | Diesel Price in Gurgaon | CNG Price in Gurgaon | LPG Price in GurgaonStay updated with the latest Gurgaon news. articles.title: Empregados da Caixa rejeitam proposta final e greve continua | G1
articles.standfirst: Na base de São Paulo, Osasco e região, 68% votaram contra o texto apresentado pelo banco. Segundo o sindicato, paralisação é nacional e segue por tempo indeterminado.
articles.summary: Na base de São Paulo, Osasco e região, 68% votaram contra o texto apresentado pelo banco. Segundo o sindicato, paralisação é nacional e segue por tempo indeterminado.
articles.body:
Greve de bancários da Caixa em Araraquara (SP) — Foto: Sindicato dos Bancários/Divulgação

Os empregados da Caixa Econômica Federal rejeitaram a proposta final apresentada pelo banco para a renovação do Acordo Coletivo de Trabalho (ACT) . Com a decisão, a greve iniciada na quinta-feira (10) continua por tempo indeterminado.

Segundo o Sindicato dos Bancários de São Paulo, Osasco e Região, a paralisação é nacional. Na base da entidade, a assembleia terminou às 23h desta sexta-feira (11), com 68% dos votos contrários à proposta.

O texto havia sido apresentado pela Caixa após a retomada das negociações com as entidades que representam os funcionários, numa tentativa de encerrar a greve.

A proposta previa, entre outros pontos, um prêmio de R$ 3 mil por empregado, além do pagamento, em 18 de setembro, do salário reajustado, da Participação nos Lucros e Resultados (PLR), do Super Caixa e do prêmio.

Também estava prevista a ampliação de 6,5% para 8% do limite de participação da Caixa no custeio do Saúde Caixa, plano de assistência médica dos funcionários. O benefício está entre os principais pontos de divergência entre os trabalhadores e o banco.

Caixa havia indicado possibilidade de levar negociação à Justiça

Antes da votação, a Caixa informou que aquela seria sua proposta final e que, caso os trabalhadores não aprovassem os termos dentro do prazo, poderia retirar a oferta e ingressar com um dissídio coletivo, levando a negociação para a Justiça do Trabalho.

O banco já havia informado que mantinha o diálogo aberto com as entidades representativas dos empregados e que havia retomado as negociações em busca de um acordo.

A paralisação começou na quinta-feira (10), depois que os trabalhadores rejeitaram uma proposta anterior para a renovação do ACT.

Segundo a Confederação Nacional dos Trabalhadores do Ramo Financeiro (Contraf-CUT), mais de 90% das bases sindicais rejeitaram o texto anterior apresentado pela Caixa.

Com a nova rejeição nesta sexta, a greve permanece por tempo indeterminado.

A Caixa informou anteriormente que os clientes podem continuar utilizando os canais digitais e remotos, como App Caixa, Internet Banking, WhatsApp Caixa e Caixa Tem, além de caixas eletrônicos, Banco24Horas, lotéricas e correspondentes Caixa Aqui.

articles.title: Jarbas Dias Ferreira: veterano da 2ª Guerra morre aos 104 anos | G1
articles.standfirst: Tenente Jarbas Dias Ferreira, que lutou na Itália pela Força Expedicionária Brasileira (FEB), morreu nesta sexta-feira (11), aos 104 anos, em São José dos Campos.
articles.summary: O veterano da FEB Jarbas Dias Ferreira faleceu em São José dos Campos, deixando um legado de bravura nas trincheiras da Segunda Guerra Mundial na Itália.
articles.body:
O tenente Jarbas Dias Ferreira carregava na memória histórias da guerra que atravessaram mais de oito décadas. Veterano da Segunda Guerra Mundial, ele passou um ano em solo italiano, enfrentou noites em trincheiras, frio extremo e do sofrimento provocado pelo conflito.

Jarbas morreu nesta sexta-feira (11), aos 104 anos, em São José dos Campos, no interior de SP. A Prefeitura decretou luto oficial de três dias pela morte do ex-combatente da Força Expedicionária Brasileira (FEB).

“Infelizmente a guerra é a pior coisa que existe. Não existe coisa pior do que uma guerra”, afirmou.

Tenente Jarbas Dias Ferreira em evento do tiro de guerra. — Foto: Prefeitura de São José dos Campos/Arquivo

Jarbas atuou na guerra quando ainda era jovem. Durante o período em que esteve na Itália, passou oito meses em combate. Na época, atuava como cabo e tinha sob sua responsabilidade uma metralhadora e uma equipe de seis homens.

Entre as lembranças mais marcantes estavam as condições enfrentadas pelos soldados. O frio era intenso e, segundo ele, chegou a passar noites com temperaturas de 20°C negativos.

“[Lembro de] passar a noite a 20 graus abaixo de zero. Não passei fome. Dormia um pouco, até na trincheira”, contou ao g1.

Ao falar sobre os civis, contou que viu crianças, adultos e idosos passando fome e enfrentando situações de extrema dificuldade.

Entre tantas lembranças, uma data permanecia especialmente viva para Jarbas: 8 de maio de 1945, o chamado Dia da Vitória, quando a Alemanha nazista se rendeu.

O fim do conflito representava, para ele, a possibilidade de finalmente voltar para casa e reencontrar a família.

“Foi o dia mais feliz da nossa vida, porque a gente tinha certeza de que viríamos logo para a nossa casa”, disse na entrevista ao g1 .

Tenente Jarbas Dias Ferreira era um dos remanescentes da Força Expedicionária Brasileira (FEB). — Foto: Reprodução/Rede Vanguarda

Nascido em Mogi das Cruzes, no Alto Tietê, em 1921, Jarbas chegou a São José dos Campos em 1934, ainda jovem.

Ele trabalhou na Tecelagem Parahyba antes e depois da guerra. Mais tarde, tornou-se comerciante e ficou à frente da tradicional Bicicletaria Brasil, na avenida Rui Barbosa, no bairro Santana, na região norte da cidade.

Mesmo depois de deixar o serviço ativo, manteve uma relação próxima com o Exército Brasileiro. Era presença frequente nas cerimônias de formatura do Tiro de Guerra de São José dos Campos .

Nas solenidades, fazia questão de cumprimentar os jovens que iniciavam ou concluíam o serviço militar obrigatório.

A Prefeitura de São José dos Campos decretou luto oficial de três dias pela morte do tenente Jarbas Dias Ferreira.

O velório aconteceu na Urbam (Urbanizadora Municipal), na Vila Industrial, e o tenente foi enterrado no Cemitério Municipal Padre Rodolfo Komorek, no Centro de São José dos Campos .

articles.summary: Série acontece nos dias 14 e 15 de setembro e terá dois candidatos às eleições de 2026; entrevistas serão exibidas pela TV Globo e pelo g1.
articles.body:
O governador Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos) escolheu Osasco, na Grande São Paulo, para iniciar a corrida pela reeleição. Fernando Haddad (PT), por sua vez, ainda não fez seu evento próprio de lançamento, mas começou a campanha ao lado do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), em São Bernardo do Campo, no ABC Paulista. — Foto: Montagem/Estadão Conteúdo

A Globo realiza, em 14 e 15 de setembro, uma série de entrevistas com candidatos ao governo de São Paulo nas eleições de 2026 . As conversas sobre os principais temas do estado serão exibidas ao vivo diretamente dos Estúdios Globo, em São Paulo.

A Globo convidou os dois candidatos mais bem colocados na pesquisa de intenção de voto divulgada pela Quaest em 8 de setembro. A ordem das entrevistas foi definida por sorteio, com a presença de representantes dos partidos.

14 de setembro (segunda-feira) : Fernando Haddad ( PT )

15 de setembro (terça-feira) : Tarcísio de Freitas ( Republicanos )

As entrevistas serão exibidas no SP1. Além da TV Globo, o público poderá acompanhar a transmissão pelo g1. Depois da exibição, o conteúdo ficará disponível na íntegra no Globoplay e no g1 .

As entrevistas serão conduzidas pelo jornalista Alan Severiano.

articles.title: Why brazen museum thefts keep happening nearly a year after Louvre heist
articles.summary: Art detectives and security experts say the number of museum thefts across Europe is increasing.
articles.body:
When thieves broke into a French museum earlier this week and stole four paintings by the impressionist artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir, worth millions of euros, not everyone was surprised.

Just last month, the European policing agency (Europol) had warned that museum thefts across Europe were growing increasingly brazen.

And just days before the Renoir heist, internationally known art detective Arthur Brand predicted to the BBC that more high-profile burglaries were likely - particularly in the wake of the successful robbery at the Louvre in Paris last October .

The audacious crime in one of the world's most famous museums stunned France, and the stolen jewellery worth €88m (£75m) has still not been recovered, nearly a year on.

"We will see more of this," says Brand, "because if you are able to hit the Louvre, thieves all around the world are watching that, thinking, 'Wow' - and then they think, 'Don't we have a local museum with gold and silver?'".

Within hours of the Louvre burglary, thieves had raided coins from a smaller museum in France. Since then, criminals have stolen a diamond necklace in Vienna , Bronze Age artefacts in Spain , and art from two Italian museums - and that's only what the BBC has written about.

The heist at the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer is the latest, and detectives are still working to track down the remaining multi-million-pound paintings - two of which were quickly recovered after thieves dropped them in the museum garden.

Europol tells the BBC the number of museum theft cases reported to them across Europe began to increase about two years ago.

Its recent report says both the methods and targets of thefts are changing - with a rise in more forceful tactics, and, as in the Louvre case, a focus on high-value items such as precious metals and gemstones.

Both Brand and Ibrahim Bulut, a museum security expert from a Belgian security consulting firm, believe many thefts that followed the Louvre burglary are copycats.

"Every museum in the world is stressing now," Brand says. "In every museum there have been meetings with the security officer or with the police."

From tiaras to Bronze Age rings: Stolen museum treasures

The Association for Research into Crimes against Art (ARCA) says the recent thefts show "a repeated preference for small, portable, immediately accessible objects and for attacks designed to be completed in minutes".

Data provided to the BBC by ARCA shows recorded museum thefts in France spiked in 2024, and rose again slightly in 2025.

However, numbers go up and down over time, with more thefts recorded in 2015 than a decade later.

These crimes threaten what many consider invaluable artefacts of historical and cultural value enjoyed by the public - although some people argue they steal "from the rich, who cares?" Brand says.

Others point out the colonial history behind many treasures in European museums, with art historians highlighting the French crown jewels stolen from the Louvre contained emeralds, diamonds, sapphires and pearls which are not native to France.

Museums are vulnerable and easy to burgle, Brand says, compared to well-secured jewellery shops and banks - which these days hold less cash.

Directors historically "never have enough money for security" or prefer to spend it on the next exhibition, and museums are often housed in old buildings that are difficult to protect, he adds.

For example, the Denis Diderot Maison des Lumières (House of Enlightenment) - burgled hours after the Louvre - is housed in two 18th-century mansions in Langres.

"We therefore have to reconcile modern security requirements with the need to preserve historic buildings and comply with France's heritage regulations," local mayor Théo Caviezel explains.

Museums are also open public spaces that have less access control and perpetrators can come in as visitors, says Kumar Sokka, CEO of Acre Security which works with some museums in Europe.

And even if a museum is secured well, thieves could still come in armed, Brand says, adding that it would be impractical to put police in galleries.

Many of these burglaries are over in minutes and the thieves have long gone by the time police show up - the Renoir case happened within five minutes.

Heists used to depend on deception, but burglaries are now becoming increasingly violent, Europol's report last month points out. Offenders are using tools such as sledgehammers, axes, crowbars and, in some instances, explosives, to get inside.

In the Louvre, the thieves used a mechanical lift to gain access, cut through the window with power tools and then threatened guards, who left, before forcing their way inside displays and grabbing the jewels. In the Renoir case, the perpetrators used an electric knife to cut through a fence before sawing through structures holding the paintings' frames in place.

The increased aggression creates new security concerns.

"An armed incident during opening hours, like the one we experienced, creates a situation in which the immediate priority is to keep our audience and staff safe," says Lilli Hollein, the director of the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK) in Vienna, which was burgled last month.

What is being stolen is also changing. While paintings are still taken, they're harder to sell, so around 10 years ago, thieves began shifting to goods that are easier to get rid of, Brand says.

Now precious metals, gemstones, and culturally significant artefacts including Chinese porcelain are increasingly targeted, according to Europol's report.

"Precious metals can be easily melted down, leaving no trace for law enforcement, and facilitating illicit sales during the fencing process," it says. "Precious stones in jewellery, on the other hand, can be easily removed and sold further."

Meanwhile, Chinese porcelain is likely to be easily sold on the art market because of high demand, Europol says.

After a theft, police generally have between four to six days to catch the thieves, according to Brand, who works with investigators by calling informants and receiving tips from the public or even ex-partners of perpetrators.

But while suspects may be arrested, jewels or precious metals might not be found - such as with the Louvre case.

On the other hand, Brand believes the Renoir paintings stolen this week - two of which were dropped by the thieves on their way out - "will probably be recovered" because "no one will want to buy" them and "it is likely, then, that the thieves have no idea what to do with them".

Christopher A. Marinello, the boss of Art Recovery International that recovers stolen art, says only 5-10% of stolen art is ever recovered, making thefts from small museums like this week's "extra painful".

Tuesday's heist is another example of "Europe's museums under siege", he adds.

After its theft in October, Maison des Lumières launched a security audit carried out by police officers appointed by France's cultural ministry, mayor Caviezel says.

Some recommendations are already being implemented, such as enhanced video surveillance, while other structural improvements are in the process of being developed.

MAK in Vienna also increased its security to prevent "copycat offenders and to provide our audience with visible security", its director says. Entry is through a metal detector, and bags must be put in the cloakroom or in lockers, and there are more security guards.

Experts say the trick is to create physical barriers that will delay thieves so there is time for the police to arrive, or to make any theft take so long that it would deter would-be offenders from attempting it.

"Security is about buying time", says Bulut. "The objective is not to make the theft theoretically impossible, but to make removal difficult, noisy, detectable and above all, time-consuming, because to be very honest, thefts can always happen, it's the timing that you're concerned about."

Brand says a delay could be building an extra, heavy door anchored into the ground, thickening the glass on display cases or using a fog machine.

Sokka says it's critical to have integrated systems - so for example if an alarm goes off, you could shut down the facility, or lock down all high net worth paintings.

However, security measures are expensive. Mayor Caviezel, whose small French city hosts two museums and collections, says finding the money is "one of our main challenges".

"A small city can be entrusted with collections of national importance without having the financial resources of a major Parisian institution."

Bulut, who sits on the International Committee for Museum Security board, says it's not all about expensive gadgets. It could also be training guards to spot suspicious people who may be casing a museum and ask them if they need help, which may deter them from returning.

Museums are investing: Sokka says his company has seen an uptick in seismic offerings, that can detect vibration such as drilling in walls, in the past 18 months.

Museum heists are not increasing everywhere in Europe. In Sweden, major museum thefts began to decline around a decade ago and have not changed significantly in recent years, said Peg Magnusson, Sweden's representative for a UNESCO convention to combat illicit trafficking of cultural property. However, other worrying cultural artefact targets have emerged.

The challenge for museums now is increasing security while also staying open to the public.

"A museum cannot be a fortress," Hollein says. "We want to be open institutions; at the same time, we are facing new challenges and attacks against museums that will require new standards."

articles.title: Passenger train derails in France, leaving 44 injured, 1 critical
articles.summary: French train derailment sparks emergency response, with 130 firefighters and five medical teams dispatched to the scene.
articles.body:
A passenger train derailed in northwestern France on Friday, injuring 44 people, one critically, local authorities said

The train, which was carrying 186 passengers, was travelling on Friday between the Normandy cities of Rouen and Caen when it derailed at about 7:45pm (17:45 GMT), French Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot said on X.

Local authorities said they had activated a mass-casualty response plan, deploying 130 firefighters, five medical teams and 80 vehicles to the scene.

Rouen prosecutor Sebastien Gallois said 44 people were injured, including an 18-year-old woman who was evacuated in “critical condition”.

According to the prefecture of Seine-Maritime, the young woman was evacuated by helicopter to Rouen University Hospital.

One passenger, Louis, 24, told local radio ICI Normandie: “Suddenly there were a few jolts, and then after about three seconds it got stronger and stronger.”

He added, “I couldn’t stay in my seat any more. The windows partially shattered, the stones from the track came into the carriage. It was really shocking. I’m still shaking.”

SNCF Reseau, which manages France’s rail network, said traffic on the line had been suspended and power to the tracks was cut to allow emergency services to operate.

“The priority is to care for the passengers and then to restore safe operating conditions,” the company said.

Gallois said tests for drugs and alcohol on the train driver had come back negative.

Rail authorities and police are investigating the cause of the derailment.

articles.title: I couldn't experience my baby scan but blind parents like me can now feel them
articles.summary: New innovations and workarounds are constantly being made to support blind parents in the challenges they face.
articles.body:
When I attended pregnancy scans a decade ago, the best the sonographer could do to involve this blind expectant mum was to turn up the volume on the heartbeat.

But now, parents like me can receive tactile 3D models created from their scans, allowing them to have a special moment with their unborn baby.

Reece Finnegan-Knight, who has been blind since his teens, is one of the first people to experience a 3D-printed model of his baby's scan with his wife, Sophy, as part of a new pilot scheme.

At their routine 12-week scan, Sophy had attempted to describe what she was seeing for Reece, but he struggled to feel involved in the moment.

Afterwards, when the couple showed the sonogram to their loved ones, Reece said it felt like "friends and family knew more about my baby than I did".

But he said the 20-week scan was more positive.

"The sonographer described everything to me, and explained why what she was seeing meant that everything looked good," he says.

They also now have the model of their 20-week scan picture, through the scheme by the charity Guide Dogs.

"I can't stop feeling it to be honest," Reece says.

"It's so nice to be able to fully access something without the need for other people's descriptions or interpretations. It has enough detail that I know what things are and it just makes everything feel more real."

It's an innovation which has made me reflect on my own experiences of pregnancy and parenting.

Before my partially sighted husband and I started trying for kids, I researched absolutely everything it would entail, from how to use specialist apps to read pregnancy test results, to the bells and squeaky shoes I could use to keep tabs on a fast-moving toddler.

I immediately discovered a community of people in my position ready to share their wisdom, and a host of tried and tested workarounds for almost every scenario.

But a decade on, there are even more advances, and I've spoken to other blind parents to find out the best ways they tackle the challenges they face.

For Kim and Sean Randall, who have a teenager and an 11-month-old, the progress of technology is one of the biggest changes they have noticed in the 15 years between the births of their children.

For their youngest child, maternity notes came in an app which could be accessed with a screen reader on their phone, rather than being handwritten in the traditional NHS blue book.

Kim says it put her on more of an equal footing with other expectant parents, and helped her feel more in control.

"I could check the notes, and any test results, when I wanted rather than waiting to have them read to me," she says.

For the 20-week scan, she says Sean had researched the meaning of the different numbers on an ultrasound - like the baby's thigh length or head circumference - and used a specialist AI screen-reading app to have the text read out and the images described.

Some parents say they prefer this method to a 3D model, because they can get more detail from audio description of the image than from physical touch.

But it's not just scans where visually impaired parents can struggle.

Reece, like many blind parents, says he wants to be extra prepared for when the baby comes, "so I don't get in the way or feel like a liability".

"We've been labelling clothes, putting Braille in baby books and organising the baby bag so that I know where everything is," he says.

Kim, meanwhile, runs Facebook and WhatsApp groups for blind mums. Together, we have collated a host of tips and tricks from blind parents over the years for what to do when the baby arrives.

Carry your own folding mat for nappy changes and always have everything you need close at hand

When changing a nappy, if you think you can stop, "keep wiping" - and use barrier cream, because the start of a nappy rash can be hard to feel

Score a raised mark on any syringes or scoops you might use for making up feeds so you know where to fill them to

Use a baby carrier or pram which can be pulled as well as pushed, in case you walk with a guide dog or cane in front of you to get around

Once they start toddling, bells clipped to clothing are a handy way of knowing where they are at home

When weaning, use a wipeable high chair with a waterproof mat underneath, to keep mess contained and know what they've eaten and what's gone on the floor

The Royal National Institute of Blind People (RNIB) has also produced guides for expectant parents and those with young children.

They suggest ideas like using baby gates to block off the kitchen when you are removing something from the oven, or the hall when you are answering the door.

For parents who have some but not total visual impairment, Kim says children can be dressed in brightly coloured clothing while out and about so they are easier to spot.

"I put them in feelable clothes so I don't grab the wrong child," says Kim, who has no vision.

"One of my favourites is a shirt with a castle on it. You open the door and there's a dragon inside."

When her eldest started walking, she says "we always held hands, but had a wrist strap connecting us in case she tried to run off".

For me, clothes pegs were always useful for keeping outfits together wherever possible.

Also consider buying socks the same style and colour - matching those is still a nightmare for me a decade later. If two items feel the same but are different colours, cut the label on one of them.

Parents Reece and Sophy are just at the start of their journey, but are making sure they are fully prepared for what lies ahead.

As the due date rapidly approaches, they were given a hospital tour as an accessibility requirement.

For Reece, knowing his way around the maternity ward beforehand means he can be "more independent and able to support Sophy as her birthing partner".

My own children are older now, and I look back at those early years with gratitude for the blind parents before me who figured out the workarounds and gave reassurance when others' attitudes or new challenges caused me to lose confidence.

I now pay that forward whenever possible. For blind parents, that community exists and is ready to be a source of support.

And remember, when you think you can stop, always keep wiping.

articles.title: Sweden election becomes tight race, as hard right eyes role in government
articles.summary: Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has promised cabinet jobs for the Sweden Democrats, but the rival left-wing bloc has a narrow lead in the polls.
articles.body:
Sweden's left- and right wing political blocs are in a tight race in Sunday's general election, with current conservative Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson promising cabinet jobs for hard-right allies if he remains at the helm.

Latest polls show a narrow lead for the left grouping, which is backing the Social Democrats' Magdalena Andersson to return to power.

Kristersson has been supported in government by the hard-right Sweden Democrats (SD), who have neo-Nazi roots.

National security, gang crime and welfare spending are among the key issues, but the potential for the anti-immigration SD to enter government could also influence the outcome.

In Sweden, there are two major political blocs - with four parties on the right and four on the left, so Swedes are used to coalition and minority governments.

More than eight million people are eligible to vote in the election for Sweden's Riksdag.

A poll on Friday, commissioned by Swedish news service Ekot, shows the left-wing bloc with 50.8% of the vote, compared with the right-wing bloc on 47.6% - a lead of 3.2%.

The centre-left Social Democrats, who have pledged higher public spending, lead the polls, with 28.6%, while on the right the Sweden Democrats are behind them with 18.3%, according to the Ekot survey.

Other opinion polls on Friday also put the left-wing bloc in the lead.

The Social Democrats have regularly led Swedish governments since World War Two and have been the country's dominant political force for much of the last century.

In stark comparison the SD, founded by Nazi sympathisers in the 1980s, were for decades shunned by the mainstream.

But the last election in 2022 marked a watershed moment , with the SD becoming Sweden's second largest party following a campaign focused on issues around immigration and violent crime.

They have since offered outside support to the current centre-right coalition , which has overseen a dramatic tightening of migration policy, including the abolition of permanent residency for refugees and increased deportations. But the party's MPs have never held ministerial roles.

The Sweden Democrats have experienced controversies during this election campaign, including allegations that a party official spread pro-Russian messages on social media.

Kristersson has said the official should be fired if the claims turn out to be true, while SD leader Jimmie Åkesson said the party was investigating the allegations.

Nicholas Aylott, associate professor of political science at Södertörn University, told the BBC that the party getting into government "would be another big step in the normalisation of the party", but added that it was not the main issue for voters.

"That said, it might still be important for the election outcome," he said.

Aylott explained that some voters who would have backed centre-right parties may well switch allegiance to the opposition, because they are put off by the prospect of SD ministers.

Although he thought they would be few in number, "they might just tip the balance against the incumbent right-wing bloc", he said.

This weekend's election comes a week after Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) came close to winning a majority in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.

They topped the poll with almost 44% of the vote, and their local leader Ulrich Siegmund says he is in talks with another party and other MPs in the hope of taking control of parliament.

articles.title: Firefighters say glutathione helped them - their union warns it could be risky
articles.summary: Glutathione, an antioxidant, has been offered as a treatment at some of the largest US wildfires in recent years.
articles.body:
Days after he helped extinguish the Eaton Fire in Los Angeles, Pasadena Fire Captain David Marquez inhaled his first dose of glutathione on the side of the road outside the Rose Bowl stadium.

The wildfire became the second most destructive fire in California's history, killing 19 and destroying 9,000 buildings.

"We were having trouble sleeping," he said of his team. "Chronic cough, headache, fatigue - just a really rough set of symptoms following the fire."

"I felt much better immediately after the worst exposure of my career," said Marquez, a 25-year veteran of firefighting, who has battled with health issues for years.

"We were so desperate because of how messed up we were. We were willing to pretty much try anything," he said.

Scientists have long known that inhaling toxic smoke from a fire can cause a huge range of illnesses, including several types of cancers. First responders, like firefighters, are especially susceptible. Firefighters have a 14% increased risk of dying from cancer compared to the general American population, according to the US National Institute for Occupational Health and Safety.

And as awareness of the risks evolve, so too has interest in alternative - but often unproven and potentially dangerous - treatments.

Glutathione, an antioxidant that is naturally produced inside the human body, has been offered as a treatment at some of the largest US wildfires in recent years – including most recently in Spokane, Washington. Anecdotal evidence gathered by clinicians and fire departments has shown promising signs that it could be used to rid firefighters of some of the cancer-causing chemicals they absorb during fires. However, no large-scale research has yet been conducted on its safety and efficacy, and there are concerns over purity and contaminated supplies.

The International Association of Fire Fighters (IAFF) issued a rare warning about glutathione last month. It noted two recent recalls due to contaminants at compounding pharmacies that produce glutathione. It also noted scientific trials of other common, naturally-occurring vitamins that were found to increase – rather than decrease – the risk of cancer, although none of those vitamins are used in glutathione treatment.

"We don't know if glutathione is affective," said Sean DeCrane, the assistant to the general president for health and safety at the IAFF, which represents over 360,000 firefighters across the US and Canada.

"We don't know if it's a placebo effect. We don't know the long-term effect of this type of treatment."

DeCrane said his group opposes the way it has been "marketed" to firefighters, including in Spokane where morning briefings fire chiefs to their crews included suggestions that they visit a volunteer tent for treatment.

"The lack of research really raised concerns for us," he said. He adds that the IAFF has spoken to "multiple members who said that they did not feel well after the treatment, [and] that they felt worse."

"The clinician told them, 'Oh, that's just those metals leaving your body'," he said.

The recent rise of glutathione can be traced back to 2017, when a group of naturopaths formed together in Santa Rosa, California, to provide assistance to fire crews combating the Tubbs Fire.

The Integrated Health Action Network (IHAN), previously called the Integrative Healers Network, now sends volunteer clinicians to major wildfires across the country to provide glutathione, as well as other naturopathic treatments including acupuncture and massage therapy.

In response to the warning from IAFF, the group released a statement agreeing with the need for further testing, and offering to work with researchers to prove glutathione's effectiveness.

Co-founder Jen Riegle, who is not a medical doctor but is a licensed naturopath , said that glutathione treatment often leads to "clinically-meaningful improvements in headaches, fatigue and brain fog, which are some of the top symptoms we see in firefighters when they're on a fire". The treatments help to force out some of the harmful contaminants in firefighters' bodies, she claims, and can have short-term side effects immediately after treatment.

Riegle is hopeful the data the group has collected will spur on further research, and "to prove that this is a good long-term solution for firefighters". But she adds that all of the evidence IHAN has collected is anecdotal, and far from conclusive.

"I just want to be really clear that what we are collecting is data that we have because of a treatment programme," she said.

"It shouldn't ever be misconstrued as clinical trial data, or double-blind, placebo-controlled, peer-reviewed data. It is just meant as a starting point to be able to garner support for future studies." Medical trials of a new drug typically take years before receiving regulatory approval, and involve rigorous a research and standards.

Interest in glutathione rose last year when California's state Board of Pharmacy attempted to pass new rules that would have severely restricted its production.

The proposed rule change led to a groundswell of opposition from some firefighters, who travelled to the state capital to testify about how it has improved their health. The plan to further restrict it was later abandoned.

Marquez was among the firefighters who went to Sacramento to testify in uniform. He said he is grateful that glutathione is being offered more frequently – including by all fire stations in Pasadena, where he works.

He dismisses concerns about its effectiveness, including suggestions that alleviated symptoms could be due to a placebo effect.

Using an expletive, Marquez said: "I don't [care] it's a placebo - it was working. Guys were saying they felt better. I felt better. And it made me want to seek out more treatments."

Regulations and medicines for firefighters have at times lagged behind the need. Until last year, firefighters for the National Forest Service were banned from wearing face masks due to concerns about their ability to operate in rugged mountain terrains. There is now a growing understanding of the need for respiratory protections and decontamination to help prevent certain cancers that are more common for firefighters.

Dr Coralynn Sack, an occupational pulmonologist specialising in air pollution's effects on the body at the University of Washington, said the noxious fumes from wildfires are well known to pose "inhalational hazards" to firefighters.

"There's been a lot of interest in using antioxidant supplements for air pollution in general," she said. "Studies have shown mixed responses. Some have even shown worse responses."

Sack said there was "biological plausibility" to think such a treatment might work, but said she was "very underwhelmed by the data that exists". There have been no clinical trials on glutathione in firefighters, she added.

Sack said the debate over glutathione "shifts the emphasis away from things that we know work" like giving firefighters access to good personal protective equipment.

Greg Fonts, a fire captain in West Sacramento and vice-president of his local IAFF chapter, said there is a growing understanding of the importance of firefighter health. Gone are the days of not decontaminating equipment, leaving the ashes on helmets and jackets, in order to boast of past infernos.

"When I got the fire service in 2000, I would say that was the attitude was cancer was just part of the job."

"Culture has changed drastically," said Fonts, who also has been treated with glutathione. "Younger firefighters are taking health way more seriously."

articles.title: 'Yemen fighters used AI to seek guided weapons'
articles.summary: Middle East News: A group in Yemen attempted to use Anthropic's Claude chatbot to build guided rockets and missiles, the US firm has revealed, as Iran-backed Houthi reb.
articles.body: A group in Yemen attempted to use Anthropic's Claude chatbot to build guided rockets and missiles, the US firm has revealed, as Iran-backed Houthi rebels are on the offensive in the country. In a report published Thursday on how it had prevented illegal uses of Claude in several countries, Anthropic said it had "identified a cell of threat actors based in northern Yemen running three weapons development programs".Those were "a guided rocket that used a commodity phone-class flight computer with final-phase homing guidance; a multi-stage ballistic missile with a stated range goal above 2,000 kilometres; and a multi-variant missile... that included a hypersonic glide vehicle variant".The cell used Claude to develop guidance, navigation and control software for the airborne weapons that would have otherwise required a team of engineers. "We do not have evidence the actors succeeded in fielding an operational device; but they did test-fire a guided rocket," Anthropic said. "This field test appears to have failed: within hours."Anthropic said it had banned the relevant accounts as soon as it had detected the illegal activity. While the company did not identify the actors in question, it is likely to involve the Houthis.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: CIA releases dozens of declassified documents on bin Laden prior to 9/11
articles.summary: A briefer told Clinton in 1998 that bin Laden’s ‘preferred option is to strike the US on its own soil in Washington’.
articles.body:
Several dozen presidential briefing documents declassified on the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001, attacks detail intelligence government officials had gathered about Osama bin Laden and al-Qaeda leading up to the hijackings that killed nearly 3,000 people and upended the United States’ national security.

The documents illustrate security analysts’ tracking of bin Laden’s movements and support system, as well as concerns about possible threats to US targets. They also detail officials’ understanding of his network in the US and other countries, including how his operations were financed.

Proclaiming it “an act of exceptional transparency”, CIA Director John Ratcliffe said the documents were the agency’s single largest release of declassified presidential daily briefs — the highly classified briefings prepared by the nation’s intelligence community for the government’s most senior leaders.

The documents range from a February 1998 file, prepared for then-President Bill Clinton, titled “Terrorists Seeking WMD Capability” and mentioning bin Laden and other Islamic extremists, to a September 12, 2001, report in which a source indicated the attacks had been planned for two years and had also targeted the US Capitol.

An April 1998 document described the Taliban’s unwillingness to hand over bin Laden, at the time seen as their “guest” in Afghanistan, noting their “gratitude for his assistance during the Soviet occupation” was making them “reluctant to alienate him by monitoring or controlling his activities”.

Five months later, a briefer wrote that bin Laden’s “preferred option is to strike the US on its own soil in Washington” and that al-Qaeda “may fly an explosive-packed airplane into a US city”.

Potential hijackings were also discussed in December 1998, when a briefer described how conspirators “have evaded security checks during a recent trial run at an unidentified New York airport”, and “some members of the Bin Ladin network have received hijack training”.

Other documents detail bin Laden’s pursuit of materials for making “dirty bombs”, conventional weapons infused with radioactive material. By June 1999, according to intelligence officials, his operatives had conducted such experiments with explosives to “increase their energy output”.

Many of the documents were redacted to conceal sources’ names and other identifying information. They didn’t appear to break any new ground on the planning of the attacks or on US officials’ understanding of how they had unfolded.

articles.body: SAO PAULO — Brazilian presidential candidate Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro is under investigation for corruption, money laundering and tax evasion for receiving millions of dollars from a disgraced banker to finance a movie about his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro. Brazil’s top court unsealed several documents late Thursday that show Sen. Bolsonaro, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s primary opponent, is under investigation for receiving 61 million reais ($12 million) from a banker at the center of a corruption scandal to produce an unreleased movie titled “The Dark Horse.” The investigation, which centers on whether the Bolsonaro family misused the funds and whether the payments were properly reported to Brazilian authorities, threatens to undermine Sen. Bolsonaro’s bid for the presidency. The first round of elections is slated for Oct. 4, and the senator is locked in a tight race with Lula. The banker, Daniel Vorcaro, who was arrested in March, is accused of defrauding many of Banco Master’s 800,000 clients, including several state government pension funds, out of hundreds of millions of dollars by convincing them to make questionable investments. The scandal has engulfed several high-ranking officials in Brazil. The allegations first became public in May. Sen. Bolsonaro has denied any wrongdoing and said Friday during a campaign event in the Amazonian city of Manaus that he was seeking private investment for the movie. “It is very positive that the documents are unsealed,” Flávio Bolsonaro told journalists at the event. “I want transparency in everything. I will only confirm what I always said. There’s nothing wrong about the movie.” Corruption, money laundering and tax evasion One document alleges that Eduardo Bolsonaro, who lives in Texas and is one of Flavio Bolsonaro’s brothers, “guided how the resources (sent by Vorcaro) could be managed in the United States.” Prosecutors suspect the funds for the film were used to pay Eduardo Bolsonaro’s expenses and to promote Flavio Bolsonaro’s political agenda to the Trump administration, documents show. Eduardo Bolsonaro denied any wrongdoing in his social media channels and said investigators “are trying to repeat the mechanism that worked against Jair Bolsonaro.” The former president was sentenced by Brazil’s Supreme Court to 27 years in prison after a coup attempt. On Thursday, Brazil’s federal police seized documents from the film’s production company and from lawmaker Mário Frias, who sent about 2 million reais ($400,000) to a non-profit linked to the film. The production company and Frias deny any wrongdoing. Supreme Court Justice André Mendonca, a Bolsonaro appointee, opened the investigation into Sen. Bolsonaro in July at the request of Brazil’s federal police. Mendonca’s office has been silent about the case for many weeks, which led Lula’s allies to accuse the Supreme Court justice of shielding Sen. Bolsonaro from investigations. Mendonca unsealed the documents at the request of Chief Justice Luiz Edson Fachin, who sought to ease a political crisis within the court and bring transparency into the sprawling Banco Master probe. Fachin on Friday ordered Mendonca to release all documents regarding the Banco Master case within 24 hours. Paulo Henrique Paschoeto Cassimiro, a political science professor at Rio de Janeiro State University, said Sen. Bolsonaro’s links with Vorcaro could hurt his chances against Lula three weeks before the vote, after he spent months recovering in the polls since the revelations surfaced in May. Cassimiro added that the unsealed documents could also boost Lula’s standing since he has insisted for all of them to be aired publicly, no matter who they hit, as he knows “much of the scandal has hit politicians on the right, although not exclusively.” Lula has brought the case to his campaign in ads and recent interviews. “Banco Master was created in the Bolsonaro administration. Vorcaro was arrested in mine, the bank was shuttered in mine,” Lula said in an interview with broadcaster SBT aired Thursday evening. Brazil’s Central Bank shut down Banco Master, whose assets topped $16 billion, in November.

articles.title: Canada court overturns 'unreasonable' visitor-visa refusal for 3 Indian applicants
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In a respite for three Indian applicants whose tourist visa to Canada was rejected by an immigration officer, the Federal Court of Canada overturned t.
articles.body: In a respite for three Indian applicants whose tourist visa to Canada was rejected by an immigration officer, the Federal Court of Canada overturned the refusal, and sent the applications back for reconsideration by a different officer.In the judgement given on Sept 1, the court said that the visa officer's decision - which was based on concerns about the financial situation of the three applicants - was unreasonable. The crux of this decision is that unlike international students, visitors to Canada are not required by statute to demonstrate sufficient and available financial resources.According to Canada's 2025 Annual Report to Parliament on Immigration, India was the leading source country under the country's 'Visitor Program' in 2024, accounting for 5.8 lakh admissions, or about 11.5% of the total. Against this backdrop, the court's decision could offer some reassurance to applicants whose visitor-visa applications are refused without proper consideration of the evidence they have submitted.In this case, the immigration officer considered that the applicants' assets and finances were insufficient to support the stated purpose of their visit. Particular attention was paid to lump-sum deposits appearing in the principal applicant's bank statement, with the officer considering that there was insufficient information about the source of those funds.The court observed that while the bank statement contained a high number of entries covering the period from July 1, 2024 to Feb 23, 2025, the origins of the deposits were in fact identified in the statements.Judge Michael Battista noted: "It was open to the officer to request more information about the source of the deposits, but it was not reasonable for the officer to definitively refuse the applications based on the absence of such information given that visitors, unlike students, are not required by statute to demonstrate sufficient and available financial resources."The applicants had given detailed financial evidence setting out a substantial amount of funds and assets belonging to the principal applicant. That evidence had been certified by accountants and banking representatives. Yet the immigration officer's decision did not address this evidence. For the court, this was significant. A decision-maker cannot simply reach a conclusion while failing to respond to important evidence put forward by an applicant, the order stated.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Saudi Arabia shuts key oil pipeline as Houthis seize strategic Red Sea island
articles.summary: Middle East News: Saudi Arabia has shut down its major East-West oil pipeline after it was attacked by drones, as the widening Iran war opened another front around one .
articles.body: Saudi Arabia has shut down its major East-West oil pipeline after it was attacked by drones, as the widening Iran war opened another front around one of the world’s most important energy corridors. The pipeline, which carries millions of barrels of crude across the Arabian Peninsula, was struck on Thursday in the Riyadh and Madinah regions, leaving several people injured and causing damage that is still being assessed.The Saudi Energy Ministry said Friday that the pipeline had been shut down as “a precautionary measure” after multiple attacks. The Saudi Foreign Ministry said the strikes were carried out by several drones coming from Iraq, where Iranian-backed militias operate, and that the attacks “caused human injuries and damage.”Saudi Arabia has so far held back from retaliation after Iraq’s prime minister asked Riyadh to give Baghdad time to take action against those responsible. The kingdom said it “reserves the right to take all necessary measures to protect its sovereignty, its security, its facilities,” and its inhabitants.Pipeline hit as Red Sea route tightensBuilt in the 1980s, the roughly 1,200-kilometre East-West pipeline has become increasingly important during the Iran war because it allows Saudi Arabia to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, where tanker traffic has been severely disrupted. The pipeline runs from Saudi Arabia’s oil-producing east to Yanbu on the Red Sea coast, providing an alternative route for crude exports.The pipeline has been moving between 4 million and 5 million barrels of oil per day in recent months, equivalent to roughly 4% to 5% of global supply, according to ship-tracking companies and analysts. By early June, Saudi Arabia had more than doubled oil exports from Yanbu to more than 5 million barrels per day.An early assessment by US officials found that pumping stations located alongside the pipeline were hit. Satellite imagery showed fire and thick black smoke rising from at least one pumping station. It remained unclear how long repairs would take or whether sections of the pipeline itself had suffered damage.Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Ministry said the kingdom had chosen not to respond “at this stage” following a request from the Iraqi prime minister. Iraq condemned the attack and said it would not allow its territory or airspace to be used to launch attacks against Saudi Arabia or neighbouring countries.The Iraqi prime minister’s office also announced the dismissal of a military commander after an investigation found that the attack originated from Iraq. Two Iraqi security sources said Baghdad had additionally ordered the closure of the Shalamcheh border crossing with Iran as a precautionary measure, while a wide-scale operation was launched to track down those responsible. Houthis seize strategic Red Sea islandThe pipeline attack came as Iran-backed Houthi rebels tightened their grip on the southern entrance to the Red Sea. Yemeni government sources said the Houthis had captured Perim Island, a strategically important position in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, after also taking control of the port city of Mocha.The Bab el-Mandeb has become more significant since the war disrupted the Strait of Hormuz. Before the conflict, about 20 million barrels of oil a day passed through Hormuz, representing around a fifth of global supply. With that route disrupted, Saudi Arabia increasingly relied on its East-West pipeline and Red Sea exports.Saudi crude flows through Bab el-Mandeb had already fallen sharply because of Houthi threats. Further disruption could force oil tankers to take much longer routes, increasing shipping costs and adding pressure to global energy prices, which have already surged above $100 a barrel.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: California governor signs law to limit U-16s social media risks
articles.summary: US News: California governor Gavin Newsom signed more than a dozen new laws on Thursday that address various aspects of children's safety online, including one.
articles.body: California governor Gavin Newsom signed more than a dozen new laws on Thursday that address various aspects of children's safety online, including one that prohibits social media companies from serving addictive features to users under 16 years old. During a signing ceremony, Newsom described the restrictions as "better" than Australia's ban for all users under 16."This is about the features themselves. This is about addressing the substantive issue around the engineering. If you address that, then the age issue is not the essential issue," Newsom said. The new law defines "addictive" features as ones that are "psychologically exploitative" and prohibits social media companies from providing children with features such as infinite scroll, algorithmic recommendations and autoplay.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: North Korea fires ballistic missiles off eastern coast, Seoul says
articles.summary: South Korea said it was closely exchanging information on the launches with the US and Japan.
articles.body:
North Korea has fired ballistic missiles towards the sea off its eastern coast, according to South Korea’s military.

South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said that it detected several missiles launched from North Korea’s eastern coastal area of Wonsan about 5:20am on Saturday (20:20 GMT on Friday), which flew about 250 kilometres (155 miles). It added that it is closely exchanging information on the launches with the United States and Japan.

South Korea’s presidential National Security Office said it held an emergency security meeting with the Defence Ministry, the JCS and other relevant agencies following the launch.

The US Pacific Command said North Korea’s launch event does not pose an immediate threat to US territory or to its allies, adding that Washington remains committed to the defence of South Korea and its other allies in the region.

The missiles were launched a day after South Korea concluded five days of joint maritime drills with the US and Japan that were focused on North Korea.

Hours after the exercises began on Monday, North Korea’s defence minister, Kim Song Gi, criticised the exercise and warned North Korea was capable of taking “strong and reflective countermeasures from the standpoint of power”.

Late last month, North Korea slammed plans for the so-called Freedom Edge exercises in international waters off South Korea as a “threat” to Pyongyang and other countries in the region.

The North also fired a barrage of missiles into the sea on August 20, despite an overture from US President Donald Trump, who said he planned to meet this year with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

The August launch from the nuclear-armed North came as South Korea and the US held a shorter edition of their annual Ulchi Freedom Shield military exercises, following an order from Trump to scale back the drills .

The order from Trump, who called the exercises “inappropriate and hostile” towards North Korea, alarmed US allies in the region.

Pyongyang has long condemned US-South Korea joint exercises as rehearsals for invasion, often staging missile launches around the drills.

articles.title: A 90-foot recycled plastic bridge reached Scotland in six pieces in 2011, and ASME reported it was assembled in just 4 days
articles.summary: UK News: In 2011, a bridge made from recycled plastic crossed Scotland’s River Tweed near Edinburgh, offering an unusual alternative to conventional steel and .
articles.body: In 2011, a bridge made from recycled plastic crossed Scotland’s River Tweed near Edinburgh, offering an unusual alternative to conventional steel and timber construction. By Axion International, the 90-foot structure in the United States was divided into six sections and shipped across the Atlantic, assembled in Scotland. A year later, ASME reported that the bridge could be erected in just four days, the wider construction project taking less than two weeks. The project showed how recycled materials and prefabrication could be combined to create a full-sized road bridge while reducing the amount of work on site.Axion shipped the recycled plastic bridge in six sectionsThe decision to prefabricate the bridge was central to how quickly it could be installed. Rather than constructing the entire structure beside the River Tweed, Axion manufactured the components in the United States and shipped the finished sections to Scotland. According to The American Society of Mechanical Engineers, the prefabricated bridge arrived in six sections, allowing crews to reassemble after reaching the site.The arrangement also reduced the amount of construction work required on site. CompositesWorld reported that the six sections were transported to Scotland and that the complete project, including dismantling the old bridge, was finished in less than two weeks. The new plastic bridge itself required only four days to erect.Axion completed the bridge project in two weeksThe project was covered by ASME in December 2012, which noted how quickly the bridge could be put up. Axion president and chief executive Steve Silverman said the company completed the construction on site in two weeks, with the process of putting the prefabricated pieces together taking only four days. He described the rapid erection of a 90-foot bridge as “a major benefit”.The four-day figure was significant because it showed how prefabrication could balance manufacturing and on-site construction. Instead of spending weeks building the bridge from individual materials, much of the work had already been done before the components reached Scotland. Silverman told ASME that the approach was intended to reduce on-site downtime and costs, while the material’s relatively low weight also made it practical to transport the structure across the Atlantic.How Axion’s recycled plastic bridge was madeThe River Tweed project was part of Axion’s wider use of recycled structural composites. ASME explained that the company’s RSC technology used recycled plastic waste, including high-density polyethene, combined with glass fibres, to create construction components such as I-beams, pilings and boards. The material could also be manufactured into complete bridges or boardwalks according to a customer's requirements.The Scottish bridge was designed to meet European standards and had a load rating of 45 metric tonnes. CompositesWorld also reported that the existing masonry piers and abutments were retained because they remained in good condition, while the new bridge provided three effective spans. The project therefore combined prefabricated recycled-plastic components with existing infrastructure rather than requiring the entire crossing to be rebuilt from scratch.Axion built and shipped the bridge in sectionsThe significance of Axion’s River Tweed bridge was not simply that it was made from recycled plastic. The project also demonstrated how a lightweight, prefabricated structure could be manufactured in one country, transported to another and assembled comparatively quickly. ASME reported that the entire construction process took two weeks, but only four days were needed to erect the new bridge itself.The project also illustrated the durability claims Axion associated with its RSC material. According to Axion's press release, the bridge would not rot, rust or corrode, and it did not require painting or regular maintenance. The material was also described as completely recyclable at the end of its functional life.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Death toll from Philippines ferry fire climbs to 35, with dozens still missing
articles.summary: Access to the burnt-out boat has been slowed by toxic fumes and lingering heat, the country's coast guard says.
articles.body:
The Philippine Coast Guard says it has recovered 30 bodies from the wreckage of a ferry that caught fire this week, bringing the total death toll to 35.

More than 130 people were on board the MV June Aster when the blaze erupted on Wednesday as it neared its destination at the tourist hotspot of Coron, after departing from Manila.

Forty-three people were rescued, with many receiving treatment in hospital, and searches continue for more than 50 people who remain unaccounted for.

The country's coast guard says more bodies remain on the boat, which they were unable to board until Friday due to toxic fumes and lingering heat.

In a press conference, coast guard spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said most bodies had been retrieved from the sleeping area of the boat, which had been making a 22-hour journey.

"Agencies are currently undertaking the proper recovery and identification of the remains in accordance with established procedures," Cayabyab said.

"We recognise the grief of the families affected by this tragic incident."

Earlier, the coast guard said preliminary interviews with the survivors suggest that the fire started in the cargo hold. Some passengers were not wearing life vests, they noted.

A survivor who was hauled to safety on a rescue boat told the BBC he had heard frantic cries onboard when the fire erupted, and was trampled by panicked people as he tried to escape.

The Philippines' maritime authority is investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident.

The ferry, built in 2002, held valid safety certificates and passed an enforcement inspection in March, but investigators are looking into potential manifest discrepancies, cargo loading integrity, and crew emergency response protocols, the Palawan Daily reported.

The vessel was carrying 117 passengers and 17 crew members.

Atienza Interisland Ferries, the vessel's operator, has pledged full cooperation with the inquiry.

"Our hearts remain with the affected families, and we will not rest until all individuals are accounted for," the company said in a statement on Thursday.

articles.title: 'Only tea was good': Near Jantar Mantar, Sonam Wangchuk appeals for support to Ladakh’s fight for democracy
articles.summary: SRINAGAR: Leh Apex Body (LAB) member and climate activist Sonam Wangchuk early Saturday appealed to people across the country to support Ladakh’s figh.
articles.body: SRINAGAR: Leh Apex Body (LAB) member and climate activist Sonam Wangchuk early Saturday appealed to people across the country to support Ladakh’s fight for democracy, saying the Centre had failed to give Ladakhi leaders an assurance at the September 9 meeting that major decisions concerning land allotment and local governance would not be taken by the current administration until a democratic government was formed in the Union Territory. The founder of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), Abhijeet Dipke, supported Wangchuk, stating, “Stand with Ladakh!”“Hello friends, cockroaches, how are you? I am in Delhi and right next to the place where we spent weeks with you all, starving, yes, Jantar Mantar. But don’t worry. I am not here for any protest or fast. We came here from Ladakh for a meeting with the Home Ministry for a dialogue. The meeting has been going on for the preservation of the culture, nature and land of Ladakh, and this meeting was also part of it,” Wangchuk said in a message posted on social media early Saturday.Wangchuk shared a video of famous comedian Jaspal Bhatti, saying the meeting resulted in no new steps except fixing the date for the next meeting. “Only tea was good in the meeting, otherwise no new decision was made,” he said. He said decisions already taken, including the creation of a democratic structure in Ladakh under an assembly, were repeated. But he said the government did not provide any assurance that the process of the proposed Assembly would not be undermined by major decisions taken by the local administration and the office of the lieutenant governor in Ladakh.“We had only expected a small, legitimate assurance from the government that until a democratic structure is established in Ladakh, the UT administration should not take any major decisions that would change the face of Ladakh, whether it is land allotment or local governance. No major changes should be brought in these areas and it should be done in coordination with the democratic structure.”Wangchuk said if they get an assurance from the government within a week on the issue, they will celebrate the padyatra from September 19 to September 24 as “a memorial padyatra of the martyrs who sacrificed their lives for Ladakh.”“Otherwise, we will make it a big demonstration on behalf of the people of the entire country that justice should be done to Ladakh,” he said, adding that, as in every other state in the country, major decisions should be left to the people.On September 9, the Leh Apex Body and Kargil Democratic Alliance, the two organisations negotiating with the Union government for administrative autonomy for Ladakh, held talks with the MHA’s subcommittee in Delhi.After the talks, chief secretary of Ladakh Ashish Kundra said the Centre had agreed to have a legislative body under Article 371 in the region, but it would require a constitutional amendment with a two-thirds majority in Parliament.“There was a discussion on whether there would be direct or indirect elections of the UT legislative body through the Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Councils. Representatives of LAB and KDA said elections should be direct and a consensus was reached on this issue,” Kundra said at a press conference in Leh. “The question that remains to be answered concerns the relationship between the LAHDCs and the UT-level body. What powers will be vested in LAHDCs and what will be the jurisdiction of the UT-level body?”The chief secretary said the Centre had handed the Ladakh groups a list of eight to 10 questions to which they did not have immediate answers. “They were requested to think about those, consult the public and tell us what they think, so that we can move towards a draft by taking these issues forward at the next meeting in October,” he said.The chief secretary said the Centre did not want to impose any administrative model that was not acceptable to the people. “We want to move forward only after discussion with everyone. When in good faith and in the interest of everyone, everything is moving forward, it is the responsibility of the leadership here to create an environment of positivity among people, to give them hope that things are moving forward.”In a joint statement after the meeting, the LAB and KDA said the meeting furthered the “in-principle understanding” reached during talks on May 22 and July 3 on Ladakh’s demands, including constitutional safeguards through special provisions under Article 371. They said the MHA stopped short of guaranteeing powers across the board under Lists II and III of the Seventh Schedule, including law and order.The groups, however, expressed concern about “developments taking place with respect to formation of new districts, creation of hill councils of each of the new districts, and other” major irreversible changes being made before an elected body at the Union Territory level.LAB and KDA said they unanimously opposed what they called “irreversible changes” being made to the administrative and political setup of Ladakh before the UT-level body was formed.Ladakhi representatives have been in talks with the MHA since 2023 for safeguards covering land, jobs, culture and the environment. The MHA set up the committee on January 2, 2023, but the process stalled after four people were killed and more than 80 injured in alleged police firing on protesters demanding statehood in Leh in September last year.Wangchuk was accused of inciting the protesters. He was arrested, charged under the NSA and kept in Jodhpur jail. The Centre revoked his NSA detention in March this year. After his release, Wangchuk participated in the May 22 talks with the Centre. He was also one of the LAB representatives at the September 9 talks.Stay updated with the latest Srinagar news. Download the TOI App.
