articles.title: Mexico rescues eight from clandestine clinic run by violent Jalisco cartel
articles.summary: Rescue operation in Jalisco uncovers cartel’s hidden clinic, illegal drugs and weapons; six suspected guards arrested.
articles.body:
Mexican law enforcement has said it rescued eight people who had been forcibly recruited by the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), one of the country’s most powerful and violent drug trafficking organisations.

The eight people were found at a clandestine clinic on a farm in the municipality of Tecalitlan, in the western state of Jalisco, roughly 160 kilometres (100 miles) from Guadalajara, the AFP news agency reported.

Images released by state prosecutors showed dimly lit rooms with mattresses on the floor and heavily stained walls. One photo showed a cap bearing an image of Jesus Malverde, a folk figure widely revered by drug traffickers as an unofficial patron saint.

Jalisco state prosecutor Salvador Gonzalez said the property “operated as a place to shelter people recruited by organised crime who, for one reason or another, ended up injured in connection with the activities they were made to carry out and needed to recover”.

He added the victims “had been deprived of their freedom”. Two of those rescued were on crutches. Authorities said they also seized illegal drugs and narcotics, as well as weapons and ammunition. Six suspected guards, aged 21 to 48, were also arrested.

Investigators found the site while searching for a 20-year-old man who had gone missing in late July after leaving his home in Tlaquepaque, near Guadalajara, in a taxi to answer what he believed was a job offer at a farm.

The case echoes the 2025 discovery of a suspected CJNG training camp at a ranch in Teuchitlan, also in Jalisco, where a civilian search collective found clothing, luggage and human remains, leading to more than 40 arrests.

An estimated 134,000 people are believed to be missing across Mexico, with Jalisco having one of the country’s highest rates of missing people.

Mexico’s government said last week it had disabled more than 1,700 social media profiles spreading fake job offers to lure young people into crime.

articles.title: "Joy Is Not Something That Comes Naturally" — India Mahdavi on Evoking Emotion and Comfort in Interior Design, and Why Color Should Disturb
articles.summary: As India Mahdavi tells our executive editor, Pip Rich, joy is an emotion that can be evoked with the right color choices and a certain amount of bravery
articles.body:
When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission.

For most of our UK readers, the India Mahdavi project they're most familiar with is the (formerly) Pink Room at the Gallery at Sketch in London. Gentle yet vivid, it's a great introduction to the French-Iranian architect and designer's bold use of color.

"That space announced something publicly that I had felt privately for some time," says India. "That color could be an architectural decision, not a decorative one, and that joy was a serious ambition." And so she set the tone for her interior design, architecture, furniture, and more.

Eager to get more insight about the emotional impact of color from India , I asked her for an interview. The conversation below explores how the designer pursues joy, the different layers of comfort in interiors, and why color should disturb.

Your work is so often described as joyful. Is that a feeling that comes naturally to you?

I am always fighting my own melancholia. Joy is not something that comes naturally to me — it is something I pursue, something I build. This is precisely why I take it seriously as a design intention. Joy, for me, is not decoration. It is an act of resistance. In fact, I think joy has long been undervalued in design.

For too long, seriousness meant severity. Ornament was crime, color was frivolity. I never believed that. Today, when the future offers so little reassurance, joyful color becomes not just a value but a necessity. A serious matter, to make someone feel — even briefly — that the world is bearable and beautiful.

Habitat's new checkerboard coffee table is bold and contemporary, but in brown and cream tones if decorating with red feels like too much for your interior scheme.

I really believe that great design can do that, in the same way as art. It's so affirming.

Color is very visible and very photogenic — and in a world where the image has become so dominant, that has given it an almost inflationary quality. Everyone uses color now. Not everyone uses it with meaning. What interests me more is friction. Imperfection. The idea that a color can disturb slightly before it seduces.

I am not interested in color that simply pleases — I'm interested in color that provokes a second look, that creates a slight dissonance before resolving into something right. In difficult times, color should not offer false comfort. It should offer the kind of aliveness that reminds you that you are here.

Add a focal point above your kitchen island, like India's, with this three-light white silk pendant light.

What do you think color can do to a person's emotions?

Color brings a vibration, a quality of light that is not physical but psychological. It can produce joy, unease, nostalgia, desire — sometimes several at once. At its most powerful, it doesn't produce a single emotion but an openness to feeling. It makes you more present in a room.

A personal favorite design of yours is the Rosary headboard for Bolzan. How did you come up with that palette?

For the Rosary headboard, it was less about color choice than about meaning. I wanted to integrate something into a bedroom that could sanctify it. The bed is the center of your life in a way we rarely acknowledge: it is where you dream, where you are most vulnerable, where the most extraordinary things happen to you. It deserves reverence. The ceramic beads are there as a kind of offering — a private ritual object. And because every combination can be customized, every bed is different. Every dream is unique.

If you don't want to go as bold with a pouf, you could opt for something that gives a more subtle pop of yellow to your space, like this fun chequered design from Westwing.

So which colors are you finding yourself drawn to at the moment?

It is entirely instinctive — and yet also very precise. I know which color belongs and which does not. I often feel that colors impose themselves on me, that I am only their medium. The work is not choosing. The work is listening closely enough to hear what the space is asking for.

What resonates from your work is how integral color is. What do you think is the effect of being as bold as you are?

It can provide comfort . And I think of comfort in three distinct ways: physical comfort, visual comfort and emotional comfort. Physical comfort is the most obvious — scale, proportion, the quality of a seat. Visual comfort is subtler: the sense that wherever your eye lands, there is something worth resting on, without noise or aggression. And emotional comfort is the deepest — the feeling that this room knows you are there. That it was made with a human being in mind. Achieve all three simultaneously, and there is simply no reason to leave.

If you want more designer Q&A's, we spoke to interior designer Shalini Misra about comforting schemes, impactful curation and the power of negative space.

And for more design ideas and inspiration, subscribe to the Livingetc newsletter , and all the latest will be delivered directly to your inbox.

articles.title: The world’s deadliest sea route keeps getting busier
articles.summary: Each year, thousands of Rohingya refugees, many of them women and children, pack into the crammed cargo holds of old fishing trawlers departing from Bangladesh or Myanmar to cross rough, open waters in the Bay of Bengal and the Andaman Sea in search of safety or opportunity in Indonesia or Malaysia.
articles.body: Abdul Nur last heard from his son Jani Alom in early June, weeks before the 15-year-old boy was forced onto a boat embarking on one of the world’s most dangerous sea crossings. “Oh ba,” a teary and panicked Alom said over the phone, his father recounted to CNN. Alom used the word for “father” in Rohingya, the language spoken by the ethnic group of the same name. “I am going to be put on a boat to Malaysia.” The boy had been abducted one evening two months earlier while walking home from school in the Bangladeshi refugee camp where the family has lived for nearly a decade, alongside more than one million other Rohingya exiled from western Myanmar. The Rohingya are a stateless Muslim minority from Myanmar’s Rakhine state, who have faced decades of state-sponsored persecution, violence and what the US has classified as genocide. Each year, thousands of Rohingya refugees, many of them women and children, pack into the crammed cargo holds of old fishing trawlers departing from Bangladesh or Myanmar to cross rough, open waters in the Bay of Bengal and the Andaman Sea in search of safety or opportunity in Indonesia or Malaysia. These crossings have taken place for more than a decade but have sharply increased in recent years amid a bloody civil war in Myanmar and deteriorating conditions in the Cox’s Bazar camps, fueling a lucrative market for smugglers who facilitate these risky journeys. Before Alom made that final call to his father, Nur had collected donations from relatives and neighbors in the camp in Cox’s Bazar to pay the roughly $2,800 in ransom his abductors demanded. But his son never came home. Lost at sea Nur now believes Alom was among more than 500 people aboard two boats which vanished off the coast of Myanmar in July – the latest victims of a perilous maritime route where, according to UN figures, roughly one in seven people who attempt the trip do not make it. It’s a route which keeps getting busier. Last year, nearly 900 Rohingya refugees were reported missing or dead in the Andaman Sea and Bay of Bengal out of roughly 6,500 who attempted the crossing, which has “the highest mortality rate worldwide of any route for refugee and migrant sea journeys,” according to the UN Refugee Agency. In the first half of this year, 820 people have been reported dead or missing at sea, almost twice as many people as during the same period last year. Roughly 5,700 people have attempted the journey as of the end of June — close to the total for all of 2025. However, the numbers are only estimates because many journeys go unseen and ships sink quietly without survivors. While many go willingly, a rising number of people are being trafficked onto these ships, where abuse, exploitation and disease are rampant, according to advocates and interviews with refugee families. There has been a “significant increase in abductions” in the Cox’s Bazar refugee camp, with gangs extorting the relatives of abductees for ransom, said Chris Lewa, director of the Arakan Project, a Rohingya advocacy group. While not everyone who is kidnapped is put on a boat, she said the growth in the maritime smuggling industry has created demand for more passengers to take these risky journeys, leading to some people being trafficked. Nur said in that final call, an unknown man who he fears was a trafficker took the phone from Alom and said, “Your son has been sold here and will be sent to Malaysia.” He and his family came to Cox’s Bazar in search of safety in 2017, having escaped their village in the middle of the night and traveled for seven days on foot to reach Bangladesh, Nur said. But now he is overwhelmed with grief over the disappearance of his son, a quiet and respectful seventh-grader who loved to play football with his friends. “Every corner of our shelter reminds me of him,” Nur, 55, told CNN from his home in the refugee camp, showing the small table where his son used to study. Several camps over from Nur’s tent, through muddy paths dotted with plastic structures, another family sits in similar anguish. Hamid Ullah, 20, a teacher at the local high school, was taken from the camp at the beginning of May, his family told CNN. While they begged for money to pay an initial $1,200 ransom for Ullah’s release, they were unable to raise a further $3,200 traffickers demanded later. Ullah’s mother, Bibi Jan, said when she finally spoke to her son, he told her he was being forced onto a boat bound for Malaysia. “I asked him, “My son, will you come back? The sea is so dangerous. You could die,’” she said. The family has not received any information about Ullah since. When they later heard of the boats that disappeared, the family was stricken with grief. “Sometimes I hold and smell his shirt because it reminds me of him,” Jan said. A perilous journey The boats which recently vanished set sail from Myanmar in late June, according to a UN statement issued in mid-July. One of the ships, carrying about 250 people, lost contact shortly after departure. Another, with about 280 passengers, is believed to have sunk roughly a week later off the country’s central coast. Unlike most crossings, which take place between November and April, these ships departed during monsoon season, when the seas are prone to unpredictable storms and high swells. The passengers were mostly Rohingya people, including some who had traveled from the Cox’s Bazar camp, according to the UN. A communications blackout in Myanmar and a lack of survivors makes it difficult to get firsthand information about the ships, said Lewa. Based on discussions with her contacts, which are consistent with CNN’s interviews with victims’ families, Lewa said the passengers were taken from Bangladesh and northern Rakhine state to the village of Tha Mee Hla, along Myanmar’s Mayu River, where they waited until the boat was ready depart from the coastal village of Sin Tet Maw. The two boats departed on June 29, Lewa said. They were meant to leave earlier but were delayed due to the security situation in the war-torn state, which is violently controlled by the Arakan Army, one of the rebel groups fighting the junta. Despite the risks of sailing during monsoon season, Lewa said, she believes there was pressure from the smugglers on the boat operators to depart anyway. The first boat departed in the morning and capsized within just 12 hours, Lewa said. The bodies of approximately 10 Rohingya people who were believed to have been passengers on this boat were reportedly found along the coastline of northern Rakhine, according to various reports. Police in Bangladesh said they recovered five bodies along the southern coast in the first two weeks of July, which they said could be linked to the migrant boats, local media reported. The second boat, which left in the evening, sailed for about nine days and capsized on July 8 in the Andaman Sea, off the Ayeyarwady coast, according to Lewa and the UN statement. Lewa said she had received reports that fishermen in Ayeyarwady and Mon state, which lies further south along the coast, found several dead bodies in the ocean. The second boat may have been close to its destination in southern Myanmar, Lewa said; from there, the refugees would have likely crossed into Malaysia via Thailand through the forest. The double shipwreck comes after another migrant boat which left from southern Bangladesh sank in mid-April, leaving 250 people missing. Miraculously, nine people were rescued from the ocean. One survivor told Reuters news agency the passengers were packed into storage compartments meant for fish and nets, causing at least 30 people to suffocate to death before the boat capsized. Crisis of desperation The rising toll of people lost at sea at least partly reflects the grim conditions in Cox’s Bazar, a place that was meant to be a refuge but where rampant crime and violence, scarce resources and a lack of opportunities have made many desperate to flee – even at great risk. “They don’t see any solution for their future,” Lewa said. “So they take a chance.” Refugees are legally restricted from working or studying outside the camps, leaving them heavily reliant on international humanitarian assistance for basic needs like food. Much of this help had been coming through USAID until it was sharply slashed last year. In June the UN, in coordination with the Bangladesh government, appealed to the international community for $710.5 million to meet “the most urgent needs of Rohingya refugees and local host communities” – a “hyper-prioritized” number despite growing needs. Torrential rains and landslides frequently hit the hilly and densely populated camps, killing and displacing residents and leaving streets waterlogged for months of the year. Refugees are abducted almost every day by armed groups operating inside the camp, who kidnap people — including young children — and extort their families for money, according to reports from within the camp. Just a handful of Rohingya have been resettled in third countries like the US, and voluntary, safe repatriation to conflict-ridden Myanmar remains out of reach. “The future outlook is pretty bleak,” said Shahariar Sadat, executive director of the Centre for Peace and Justice at BRAC University in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Sadat, who oversees a research unit in Cox’s Bazar, said he’s seen firsthand the effects of overcrowding and international aid cuts on the camps, through increased crime, as well as diminished education, health care, and basic services such as food and clean water. Recently the World Food Programme cut its monthly food assistance for all refugees, giving $7 to “food insecure” households and $10 to “highly food insecure” ones while reserving the previous handout of $12 for only those marked as “extremely food insecure.” Sadat said people are often lured onto the ships by the false promise of financial stability at the other end. Refugees who reach Malaysia and Indonesia face increasingly hostile receptions and are largely banned from working; neither country is a signatory to the UN Refugee Convention. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said last month his government had struck a deal with Myanmar to take back roughly 5,000 Rohingya asylum seekers currently living in Malaysia. Shab Mia boarded the boat in the hope that he could earn enough in Malaysia to provide a better life for his 6-month-old daughter. Back at the refugee camp, his only work was carrying goods for shopkeepers and transporting relief supplies for other refugees, his wife Rubina Akther told CNN, cradling their baby inside the family’s shelter. On a good day, he’d earn the equivalent of about $1 or $1.50, she said, but many days he earned nothing at all. Mia left the refugee camp in June to return to Rakhine state, the home he had escaped years earlier. He called Akther on June 23, days before the boats left, and asked her to take good care of their daughter. She hasn’t heard from him since. “Every night, my daughter falls asleep without her father beside her,” Akther said. “She is too young to understand why he never came back, but one day she will ask me where her father is. I don’t know how I will answer her because I am still waiting for him myself. Until I know the truth, I cannot stop hoping, and I cannot stop crying.” Like Akthur, Nur can’t help but hold onto hope that his son may still be out there. “Every day we wait and pray that he is still alive.”

articles.title: ‘A f***-up of epic proportions’: Blame game begins after Iran-backed Houthis’ lightning advance down Red Sea coast
articles.summary: Desperate pleas for air cover from Yemeni generals started coming mid-morning on Thursday. As the Houthis advanced, backup support from Saudi Arabia was nowhere in sight.
articles.body: The desperate pleas for air cover from Yemeni generals started coming mid-morning on Thursday. An advance by the Iran-backed Houthis toward Yemen’s strategic port city of Mocha was in full swing, and backup support from chief ally Saudi Arabia was nowhere in sight. “The Houthis committed everything they had – waves upon waves of fighters … along with their available ballistic missiles and weapons,” a senior Yemeni source attached to their military forces told CNN. The source said he contacted the United States Central Command (CENTCOM) and was assured the US was “watching the situation closely and that Saudi air support was coming.” “But the air support never came,” the source said. “And Mocha has now fallen.” Hours later, on Friday, the Houthis captured another key coastal asset, Perim Island, at the mouth of the Red Sea. The island splits the Bab al-Mandeb Strait in two, giving Tehran de facto control over another key shipping route. The Houthis’ rapid advance amounts to an extraordinary 36 hours in a conflict that had been largely on ice for years. But the kindling for renewed fighting had been laid for months amid the conflict between the United States and Iran, as Tehran seeks to use oil prices – and their impact on the global economy – as leverage. Now, Yemen and the Red Sea have the potential to become a true second front in the Iran war. Iran’s effective control of the Strait of Hormuz plus its tightening grip on the Bab al-Mandeb Strait threatens to push oil prices even higher, weeks before November’s midterm elections in the United States. While the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the gateway to the Suez Canal shipping route, is less critical to global energy markets than Hormuz, it still carries essential goods worldwide, including millions of barrels of oil every day. The strait has become increasingly important since the start of the Iran war, as Saudi Arabia has re-routed some exports through the waterway to bypass Hormuz. “(The Houthis) don’t need to use advanced weapons to close Bab al-Mandeb. They can just use a cannon on a car,” said Amr Al-Bidh, the top official of Yemen’s Southern Transitional Council (STC). The STC has fought both the Houthis and Saudi-backed forces in the past, and wants an independent state in the south. “It’s a leverage that they have without using advanced weapons,” Al-Bidh told CNN in an interview. “And they will keep it.” ‘Ghost’ army rosters and no backup support Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman spoke twice on Thursday with US President Donald Trump and urged him to strike the Houthis, another source familiar with the matter told CNN Friday. Trump declined to intervene, according to that source. “The United States is focused on protecting our core national security interests—such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea—while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges,” the White House said in response to CNN’s questions about the calls. “We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen Government regarding regional stability.” CNN has also reached out to the Saudi Embassy in Washington for comment. The swift fall of Mocha and the lack of resistance have led to finger-pointing and recriminations among US allies. “The failure this time is not with the Yemenis,” a regional source told CNN on Thursday. “It’s a disaster made in (Washington) DC and Riyadh. The regional source told CNN that it was “a complete failure of political leadership” amid fierce squabbling and delayed decision-making in Riyadh. “There was not one air strike throughout the day yesterday (by Saudi support forces), although there were minute-by-minute updates,” the regional source added. “It’s a Saudi-American f**k up of epic proportions.” Not everyone agrees. Mohammed al-Basha, who has served as an adviser to the US government and private sector on risks emerging from the Arabian Peninsula, argues that blame also rests with Yemeni leaders, whose internal divisions jeopardized their defenses. “This goes back to a deeper problem in the anti-Houthi coalition,” the DC-based told CNN. “There is no political cohesion.” “I think everybody was aware of the Houthis’ push towards the west coast. The writings on the wall were very clear,” he added. “There’s no united command and control in Yemen.” Houthi fighters arrived in Mocha on Thursday to find Yemeni battalions that were severely depleted – their rosters were filled with “ghost names” receiving salaries, and the actual strength of the army was only about 20% of what it was on paper, a Western source with knowledge of the operations told CNN. That was compounded by the fact that the United Arab Emirates – once a member of the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen – withdrew its remaining forces from the country in January, after Saudi Arabia called for them to leave amid a dispute. And Saudi Arabia did not backfill those troop barracks and bases. “It doesn’t make sense. I mean, you have the main backer of the militaries on the ground … who are really doing all of this work for 10 years, and suddenly you ask them to leave, and you don’t fill that vacuum,” Al-Bidh of Yemen’s Southern Transitional Council added. “It’s just lack of strategy and poor management.” The senior Yemeni official told CNN on Friday that he had “warned CENTCOM repeatedly over the past few days, including yesterday, that the situation was becoming critical.” CNN has reached out to CENTCOM for response. CENTCOM chief Adm. Brad Cooper was in Saudi Arabia on Thursday for coordination meetings, two sources familiar said. CENTCOM declined to comment, citing operational security reasons. The Saudi military had been put on high alert three weeks ago, sources told CNN, but they didn’t move key air command personnel into place. The Western source with knowledge of the battle said that Saudi Arabia never deployed the necessary service personnel to control and direct combat aircraft in the event of a serious attack. “The Saudis threw the Yemenis under the bus,” the Western source told CNN on Thursday. CNN has reached out to the Saudi Arabian information ministry for comment on those allegations. The failure to defend Mocha and Perim is even more confounding in light of the recent news – reported exclusively by CNN – that more than 100 US military advisers were sent to Saudi Arabia providing intelligence and targeting support to the Kingdom in its military campaign, according to five sources familiar with the operations. The US military personnel are working as part of a newly established joint forces command, which was formed in recent weeks amid signs Iran was ramping up its own efforts to aid Houthi attacks, said one of the sources, a US official. That official estimated the total number of US personnel in Saudia Arabia at roughly 200 troops. The capture of the Red Sea assets gives the Houthis far greater maneuverability and leverage, as it opens up new locations from which the Iran-backed rebels can launch boats and attacks. Asked what comes next, al-Basha, the risk analyst, told CNN: “I think the Houthis are going to be moving east. We are seeing today, via satellite and via OSINT (open-source intelligence) photography… that the Houthis are mobilizing.” An adviser to Iran’s supreme leader on Friday described the Houthi advance on the west coast of Yemen as a “clear victory,” writing in a post on X that “the American people and Washington’s allies are paying the price for the economic crisis and Trump’s ambitions.” CNN’s Sarah El Sirgany, Mostafa Salem, Nadeen Ebrahim, Jennifer Hansler, Zachary Cohen, Katie Bo Lillis and Kylie Atwood contributed to this report.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia shuts key oil pipeline after drone attack launched from Iraq
articles.summary: Iraq removes a military commander and opens investigations into the attack that came from an area bordering Iran.
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia has closed a critical oil pipeline after it was attacked by drones launched from Iraq, as conflict in the Middle East widens.

Iraq said it had fired a military commander and launched an investigation after admitting the drone attack on its neighbour's East-West pipeline had originated in one of its provinces bordering Iran.

The 1,200km (745 mile) pipeline has helped Saudi Arabia - the world's largest crude oil exporter - bypass the Strait of Hormuz.

The incident comes amid a major advance by the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, putting more pressure on global oil shipping routes as the US-Iran war stretches into its seventh month.

Riyadh on Friday said it had shut the pipeline as a precaution, as satellite images of scorched ground and smoke near the site emerged.

The foreign ministry said the attack resulted in some injuries and damage, which was still being assessed.

The pipeline has been moving 4% to 5% of global oil supply, news agency Reuters has reported, citing ship tracking companies and analysts.

Saudi Arabia has chosen not to retaliate at this stage, its foreign ministry says, following a call from Iraq's prime minister.

It said the kingdom would "support the efforts of the Iraqi government" to "prevent attacks" launched from the country against neighbouring states.

"The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia affirms that it reserves its right to take all necessary measures to safeguard its sovereignty and security, protect its facilities, and ensure the safety of its citizens and residents," the statement added.

The Iraqi prime minister's office in its own statement said the operations commander in the Maysan governorate - a province which borders Iran - had been removed from his post following confirmation the drone attack had been launched from that region.

The Gulf Co-operation Council – made up of representatives from the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Oman, Qatar and Kuwait – also issued a missive condemning the attack.

"This attack represents a dangerous escalation and an unacceptable threat to the security of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, its territorial integrity, and its vital installations, as well as a flagrant violation of the principles of international law," secretary general Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi.

This week, a lightning advance in Yemen has also seen Houthi militants seize control of much of the country's coastline , sources say.

The group claims it has control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the gateway to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal, though it says maritime navigation is "safe for all companies except for Saudi vessels".

The developments have squeezed both sides of the Arabian Peninsula, pushing crude oil prices to over $100 a barrel for the first time since July .

articles.title: China’s Xi lands in India for BRICS summit overshadowed by wars
articles.summary: Wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, along with global energy security, are expected to dominate the summit.
articles.body:
Chinese President Xi Jinping has landed in New Delhi to attend a BRICS summit, alongside leaders from India, Russia and Iran, as wars, trade and energy test the divided grouping.

Xi departed on Saturday for the 18th BRICS summit at the invitation of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the Chinese state-run news agency Xinhua reported . His entourage includes Foreign Minister Wang Yi and high-ranking Chinese Communist Party official Cai Qi.

The conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, along with global trade turbulence and energy security, are expected to dominate the two-day meeting of the 11-nation bloc.

Xi’s visit, his first to India since 2019, will also be closely watched as the biggest step yet in the cautious thaw between the nuclear-armed rivals.

The trip comes six years after a deadly 2020 military clash along their disputed Tibetan border, with ties gradually improving through restored flights, visas and high-level contacts.

The underlying territorial dispute remains unresolved, and both sides retain heavy military deployments along their roughly 3,500-kilometre (2,175-mile) high-altitude border along Tibet.

Beijing said on Friday that it was “ready to work with India … by strengthening communication, enhancing cooperation, and properly handling differences”.

Xi is due to hold face-to-face talks with Modi later on Saturday, according to India’s Ministry of External Affairs.

“They are looking for ‘early and substantial harvest’ when it comes to the border issue,” Pradeep Taneja, a China-India expert at the University of Melbourne, said, as reported by the AFP news agency. “You cannot have a buildup of your forces on the border … but at the same time say ‘we should continue to have people-to-people relations and economic relationships.'”

Deep mistrust remains, however, with their contested Himalayan frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating ties.

Dozens of Tibetans living in exile, like their spiritual leader the Dalai Lama, protested in New Delhi on Friday, waving placards against Xi’s visit.

The Russian and Iranian presidents arrived in the Indian capital on Friday for the summit.

Russian leader Vladimir Putin held talks with Modi on Friday and agreed to further strengthen the “special” relationship between their countries.

During a meeting with Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian, Modi underscored the need to protect freedom of navigation and commerce, as well as the safety and wellbeing of ships’ crews.

India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the United States-Iran war in part by turning to Russia, despite Moscow’s war in Ukraine and pressure from Washington and other Western capitals.

BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.

articles.title: Rapper Lil Durk acquitted of murder-for-hire in 2022 Los Angeles shooting
articles.summary: LOS ANGELES — A federal jury on Friday found rapper Lil Durk not guilty of the attempted killing for hire of rival rapper Quando Rondo at a Los Angeles gas station, a shooting that resulted in the death of Rondo’s cousin.
articles.body: LOS ANGELES — A federal jury on Friday found rapper Lil Durk not guilty of the attempted killing for hire of rival rapper Quando Rondo at a Los Angeles gas station, a shooting that resulted in the death of Rondo’s cousin. The jury deliberated for three days before acquitting Lil Durk, the 33-year-old Grammy-winning Chicago hip-hop artist best known for the 2023 hit “All My Life,” of conspiracy, stalking resulting in death and murder for hire. Durk supporters including music stars Machine Gun Kelly and Ye — the artist formerly known as Kanye West — appeared in the audience during the two-week trial in downtown Los Angeles. Big groups of fans, livestreamers and other content creators gathered outside the courthouse. Durk’s co-defendants Deandre Wilson and David Lindsey were convicted of conspiracy to commit stalking, stalking using a dangerous weapon and stalking resulting in death. But both were also acquitted of murder for hire. “We thank the jury for seeing there was no murder for hire,” Wilson’s attorney Craig Harbaugh said in an email. “We are confident the remaining counts will not survive our pending motion for acquittal.” Attorneys for Durk and Lindsey did not immediately respond to emails seeking comment. Durk, whose legal name is Durk Banks, remained in custody, pending a forthcoming trial on a racketeering count that was severed from this trial. He has been jailed since his 2024 arrest. Prosecutors had alleged that Durk paid to have Rondo killed after someone from Rondo’s entourage fatally shot rapper King Von, a close friend of Durk’s and a member of his Only The Family hip-hop collective, at an Atlanta nightclub in 2020. The prosecution alleged that in August 2022, a group of men flew to Los Angeles with funds provided by Durk, followed Rondo and his crew around, and three gunmen fired on his Escalade near the Beverly Center shopping mall in Los Angeles. Rondo survived, but his 24-year-old cousin, Saviay’a Robinson, known as Lul Pab, was killed. “Today, the jury delivered justice to the family of Saviay’a Robinson, finding defendants Deandre Wilson and David Lindsey guilty of stalking resulting in Mr. Robinson’s death,” First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said in a statement. “While we are disappointed with the jury’s decision regarding Durk Banks, a.k.a. ‘Lil Durk,’ we look forward to presenting our evidence at his second trial.” Durk won a Grammy earlier that year for Best Melodic Rap Performance for “All My Life,” which features J. Cole. He has been nominated for three other Grammys and was a featured performer on Drake’s “Laugh Now Cry Later.”

articles.title: Meta glasses: Is it okay to film people in public places?
articles.summary: Meta glasses, made by the company behind Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram, have made it easier for people to film discreetly in public.
articles.body:
It's the latest wearable tech boom that is likely coming to a street, park or town square near you. But not everyone sees the future of smart glasses as rose-tinted.

The technology allows users to make calls, interact with AI hands-free and also take photos and videos simply by touching the frames, provoking concerns about privacy.

Wetherspoons, which runs almost 800 pubs across the UK, has banned using the glasses to film inside its premises and women's rights campaigners have raised issues about their potential use for harassment.

But, with videos from content creators continuing to thrive on social media platforms like TikTok and Instagram, the debate of how to best use the glasses in public places will continue to go back and forth.

Pearse Vallely is one of those content creators – the 31-year-old from Ballymurphy, in west Belfast, makes a living from his work on social media.

He uses a pair of Meta Ray-Ban glasses, with most of his videos showing his glasses-eye view of walking down the street as he greets passers-by with rhyming phrases.

One of his most popular videos, filmed in Belfast city centre, hit 600,000 views on TikTok.

The success of the videos rely on their good-natured vibe. He said he had never posted a video after being asked not to, and no one had ever got in touch to ask him to take down a video.

"I think it's because of the nature of my conversation with them. They know I'm not making an eejit out of them, I'm doing it in a positive way."

Meta glasses, the brand used by Vallely, are the market leader in the smart glasses boom, with the company saying more than seven million pairs have been sold to date.

Available for a few hundred pounds, and made in partnership with the firm behind famed sunglasses brand Ray-Bans, the frames feature an unobtrusive camera that users can activate via touch.

This turns on a pulsing white light, which aims to let people know when a video is being taken, and a flash for photos – a feature a Meta spokesperson said "smartphones and other cameras don't have".

Meta said it recently updated the glasses to disable the camera if the light was tampered with.

Should AI or smart glasses products from more companies end up selling as well as Meta's version, researchers expect as many as 100 million people will buy a pair in the next few years.

Valelly, whose videos rely on the interactions being spontaneous and natural, said people are often aware he is recording due to the light on his glasses.

He also said he tries to let people know he has recorded them after filming if he can catch them in time.

In Northern Ireland, it is generally legal to film someone even discreetly in a public place, as people in public do not usually have a reasonable expectation of privacy.

The filming would only be unlawful if it could be seen as harassment, stalking, if the footage is voyeuristic, or in circumstances where there would be a reasonable expectation of privacy.

"It's okay to have a 30-second conversation with someone," Vallely said.

"I think that's something we're losing due to technology, and I'm trying to use technology to spin it around."

Vallely said he could understand the reasoning behind banning wearing Meta glasses "if people are being crude and rude", but he said the intention behind filming was key.

"People know it's me doing it, while other people do it on troll accounts. No matter what is invented, people are going to use things for the wrong reasons."

Still, while Vallely said he hasn't run into any opposition, there are reports suggesting an increased friction between people using the glasses to film and the general public.

Last December, people hailed a woman as "a hero" after she snapped a man's Meta glasses in two on the New York subway.

In July, police in Scotland began an investigation after complaints over a TikToker who used the glasses to secret film members of the public.

Referring to the company's ban on filming, a Wetherspoons spokesperson said smart glasses breached "common sense by enabling surreptitious surveillance" while Monopoly Events, which runs Comic Con Northern Ireland, also banned wearing the glasses at its events over concerns about secret recording.

Meanwhile, TikTok videos of users approaching women, asking for their number and filming their reaction to pick-up lines, are often posted with the hashtag #howtogetagirlfriend and can garner thousands of views.

Elaine Crory, a women's sector lobbyist at the Women's Resource and Development Agency, said there's a lack of awareness about when and how the glasses are being used, leading to issues around consent.

"Right now, if you're filming with a camera or with your phone, I usually can see that and then avoid that. But you may not be aware you're being filmed with an AI camera."

She added there were also concerns the glasses were being used for things that are currently illegal, like upskirting.

Crory said people can appeal to social media sites to take videos down and some venues have put up signs "on a case by case basis", but she feels legislation has not caught up with the technology.

"A person has no legal redress if they are filmed in the street, on a bus, in a classroom," she said.

The Department of Justice (DoJ) said that while the regulation of Meta glasses was not a DoJ specific matter, if the use of the glasses involved "behaviour that crosses the criminal threshold, then existing offences such as 'up-skirting' as a form of voyeurism" were available.

For optometrist Geoff McConville, who stocks Meta glasses in his Belfast shop, there are concerns about their "inappropriate use", but there are also beneficial aspects to the technology.

He cites how his patients use text-to-speech features, allowing them to read newspapers and signs with AI.

"For my elderly, visually impaired patients, they are ground-breaking. They are amazing."

In a statement, Meta said the glasses provided "critical new technology for people who are low-sighted or hard of hearing and limiting how people can use this technology would be a major step backwards".

"Naturally some places shouldn't be filmed at all and that's reasonable but rules should be applied consistently."

In a recent Q&A session, the head of Instagram, Adam Mosseri, said if people posted content "taking advantage of people and harassing them... then we're going to take the content down".

articles.title: How a BBC strike exterminated Doctor Who adventure
articles.summary: Marcus Hearn recalls the stories his father told him about the filming of episodes in Cambridge.
articles.body:
For more than six decades, Doctor Who has taken viewers across time and space.

But hidden within the show's history are unfinished episodes recorded in Cambridge.

In 1979, production teams arrived in the university city following a storyline called 'Shada', written by local author Douglas Adams - featuring Tom Baker as the fourth Doctor.

However, not everything went smoothly during the shoot.

Speaking on a new BBC Sounds documentary Doctor Who: Lost in Cambridge , Marcus Hearn said his father, who was a porter at Clare College, saw first-hand some of the challenges the crew and Baker faced while filming.

The Doctor Who Magazine editor said: "Tom Baker had been struggling to learn how to punt and he kept falling into the Cam.

"It was my dad's job to provide him with blankets and brandy, and to basically try to calm him down because apparently he was in a very bad mood."

The story finds the Doctor in Cambridge working alongside Romana and a retired Time Lord, Professor Chronotis, to defeat the evil alien Skagra who is attempting to steal the secrets to the prison planet, Shada.

The episodes were filmed for the end of the show's 17th series.

But strike action at the BBC meant studio scenes were never completed and the episodes were abandoned .

Hearn said he had "eagerly awaited" the episodes arriving on his television after hearing of his father's adventures.

"I waited and I waited and it just never happened, so it became something of a myth and something of a legend amongst Doctor Who fans from that point onwards."

Author Douglas Adams is best known for writing the famous novel and radio series, The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.

Born in Cambridge in 1952 and educated in Essex, he returned to Cambridge to study at St John's College.

Talking about Adams, Hearn said: "This was Douglas Adams' world, of course, because he'd been a student at St John's in the early 70s.

"You can still go to St John's and look at his archive, and you could see even when he was a student and before that, he was actually writing Doctor Who stories, even before he was a professional writer."

With 'Shada' being set in and around the University of Cambridge, Hearn added: "Ironically, St John's didn't actually grant the BBC permission to shoot there and so they had to shoot at Emmanuel and Clare instead."

Richard Bignell, author of Doctor Who on Location, said crews also spent time at Grantchester Meadow

"They obviously did a little bit of improvisation as well because when the Doctor first emerges from the TARDIS when it lands, he points out, 'mind that cow pat'," he added.

Les McCallum, a design assistant on Shada, said most of the filming was completed in Cambridge, with the rest planned to be filmed in studios in London.

But, strike action cut the studio filming short, leaving the episodes unfinished.

"We did the recording in the morning and then come lunch time we all went off. We came back and all the studio doors were locked and chained because of the strike," said McCallum.

"We never saw the finished product, and they couldn't get the actors to come back again because they were contracted on other series or other shows, and that's why it never got finished."

In 1983, the show celebrated its 20th anniversary. The producer wanted to reunite all the previous Doctors in a special episode called 'The Five Doctors.' However, Baker declined.

Hearn said: "The BBC very much wanted Tom Baker to be in the show, because it was a big feature-length 20th anniversary TV movie, and then somebody remembered that they had these fragments of this incomplete story in the archive.

"So they went back to the archive, found the bits of Shada, which of course had never been broadcast, and then wrote a story around these fragments and cut them into this TV movie."

36 years after the storyline was abandoned, Baker and the cast finally returned to complete Shada.

Baker and Lalla Ward, who played Romana, recorded the missing lines from Adams' original script, and the visuals were created with animation. This new, partially animated version was released in 2017.

articles.title: BRICS meets in India: What’s on the agenda, why it matters
articles.summary: This year’s summit comes amid the US-Israel war on Iran, Russia’s war on Ukraine and global economic challenges.
articles.body:
India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi is hosting the annual BRICS Summit beginning today in the Indian capital, New Delhi, which has been decked out in BRICS-themed signs and illuminated buildings and roundabouts.

More than a dozen world leaders are attending the 18th annual summit of the bloc, which is increasingly viewed as a counterweight to economic alliances dominated by wealthier Western nations.

In preparation, some 30,000 additional security personnel have been deployed while streets around hotels the dignitaries are staying at have been closed off to traffic.

Leaders including Russia’s President Vladimir Putin, Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian and UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres arrived in New Delhi on Friday to hold early bilateral meetings with India’s Modi.

China’s President Xi Jinping, who is visiting India after seven years, arrives this morning.

This year’s two-day summit, which takes place on September 12 and 13, comes at a time of global upheaval with the United States and Israel’s war on Iran, Russia’s war on Ukraine and global energy markets in chaos.

But the bloc also faces internal challenges as differences between BRICS members over the US-Israeli war on Iran, ongoing clashes between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, and border disputes between India and China gather pace.

So how will the bloc overcome its differences this year, and what is on the summit’s agenda?

BRICS stands for Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa.

The informal trading bloc was formed in 2006, and Brazil, Russia, India and China convened for the first BRIC summit in 2009. South Africa joined a year later.

In 2023, BRICS extended invitations to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates after these countries applied for membership.

An invitation was extended to Argentina at the same time, but the South American country turned it down after President Javier Milei , elected in December, campaigned on the promise that he would bolster ties with the West.

Currently, BRICS represents 11 member countries, accounting for roughly 49 percent of the world’s population and about 40 percent of the world’s gross domestic product (GDP).

The broad aim of the alliance of governments is to challenge the economic and political monopoly of the West. The group sets priorities and holds discussions at a summit once a year, which members take turns hosting. This year’s summit is the 18th to be held.

BRICS member countries are most represented by their top leaders, including the host – Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Russia’s President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and South African President Cyril Ramaphosa. Of the original five members, only Brazil did not send its leader – President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is tied up with local elections, and Brazil will be represented by Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira.

Most newer members will be similarly represented:

Iran is represented by President Masoud Pezeshkian.

Egypt is represented by President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi.

Ethiopia is represented by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.

Indonesia is represented by President Prabowo Subianto.

While both the UAE and Saudi Arabia sent other members of government:

Saudi Arabia is represented by Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud.

The UAE is represented by the crown prince of Abu Dhabi, Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.

Other world leaders attending the summit include:

Philippines President Ferdinand R Marcos Jr

Nigeria’s Vice President Kashim Shettima

Burundi’s President Evariste Ndayishimiye

Cuba’s Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez Parrilla

Uruguay’s Foreign Minister Mario Lubetkin

Bahrain’s Foreign Minister Abdullatif bin Rashid Al Zayani

Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev

United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, the World Health Organisation’s chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and the World Trade Organisation’s Director General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala are among leaders of international organisations who are also attending the summit.

The central theme of BRICS is members’ desire to push back against the global dominance of Western-led institutions, especially when it comes to economic matters.

This year, with India hosting the summit, the theme is “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation, and Sustainability”, according to New Delhi’s BRICS presidency documents.

This year’s summit will focus on strengthening members’ economies through trade, energy cooperation, and sharing knowledge about artificial intelligence (AI) and technology.

Alicia García-Herrero, chief economist for Asia Pacific at Natixis, the French financial services group, said leaders will also discuss modes of cross-border payments amid Western sanctions on BRICS members Russia and Iran.

“But they will not try to substitute the dollar,” she told Al Jazeera.

Russia will hold discussions with other BRICS partner countries on conducting trade settlements in digital currencies at a summit this week in New Delhi, the Kremlin said on Thursday.

“These issues, which BRICS leaders will discuss, are sort of primary issues which can secure supply chains and de-risk them amid ongoing conflicts in the world,” Manoj Kewalramani, chairperson of Bengaluru-based think tank Takshashila Institution’s Geostrategy Programme, told Al Jazeera.

This year’s summit comes just more than six months since the US and Israel’s war on Iran began. In May, a BRICS foreign ministers’ meeting failed to jointly condemn the war on Iran.

Pezeshkian, who will be at the summit, is expected to discuss the war. It is his first visit to India as Iranian president and also marks the first visit by an Iranian president to the subcontinent in eight years.

“Iran is a BRICS member and the conflict has been directly affecting trade routes and energy access and market, which is having global economic impact,” Alejandro Reyes, adjunct professor in the Department of Politics and Public Administration at the University of Hong Kong, said.

But, he said, the confrontation between Iran and BRICS member UAE in the context of the war will make reaching common language on the conflict difficult for member nations.

Since the US and Israel’s war on Iran began, Tehran has retaliated by targeting US military assets and civilian infrastructure across the Gulf, including in the UAE. So far, Iranian strikes have killed 15 people in the UAE, including two military personnel, one civilian contractor and 12 other civilians. The UAE also announced an indefinite trade embargo in Iran in August.

BRICS leaders are also likely to discuss bloc member Russia’s war on Ukraine.

According to Kewalramani, however, the alliance’s leaders have been talking about Moscow’s actions in Kyiv for a few years already, and this year, he thinks they will essentially be talking about how every BRICS members’ legitimate interests around the war could be addressed jointly.

In the July 2025 joint declaration issued at the 17th summit in Rio de Janeiro, BRICS leaders avoided criticising Russia for its war on Ukraine and instead condemned Kyiv’s attacks on Russia.

“I don’t think the BRICS common language on the war this year will be problematic, given that the Americans and the Russians are talking right now,” Kewalramani added.

Earlier this month, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held talks with Putin in Moscow, in what appears to be new efforts by the Trump administration to end the Russia-Ukraine war.

Their visit came after US President Donald Trump said the envoys were bringing “a proposal to end the war” – Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II – and a senior ⁠⁠Russian ⁠⁠official said it was an “important peacemaking visit”.

What’s important about this year’s summit?

Ian Lesser, distinguished fellow at the German Marshall Fund of the United States, told Al Jazeera that against the backdrop of an increasingly fraught relationship with Europe and the US, the BRICS summit will provide Russian President Putin with an opportunity to display ties to leading countries in the Global South.

“It also offers an opportunity for Russia and China to exploit the desire of many countries to hedge against uncertain trade and security policies emanating from Washington,” he said.

This summit is also significant because of its timing: just before the second China-US summit of the year. Xi Jinping is expected to meet Donald Trump for a state visit on September 24.

Retired Senior Colonel Zhou Bo of the People’s Liberation Army told Al Jazeera that, while BRICS leaders gathering is nothing new and is part of their annual summit schedules, this year, the fact that China’s President Xi Jinping is going to India after seven years is significant.

“The relationship between Beijing and New Delhi has been frosty. So this summit is a good chance for President Xi and Prime Minister Modi to resolve differences,” he said.

Looking at the bigger picture, he said the BRICS Summit this year signals that the world order is changing amid the ongoing wars and economic challenges.

“So for BRICS in the future, there are some issues to tackle. One, which was brought up by BRICS member Brazil, is how the countries in the bloc could gradually trade in another currency and not the dollar. But that is not realistic considering there are economic disparities between BRICS countries,” he said.

“The second issue is how this organisation could play a bigger role in international geopolitics. Right now, major BRICS powers are involved in wars and finding language to comment on the wars, which is suitable for all BRICS members is going to be challenging,” he added.

What are the main divisions among BRICS nations?

According to analysts, there are substantial differences among BRICS members regarding geopolitical issues, especially after the alliance’s recent expansion.

This year’s summit comes amid an ongoing rift between BRICS members Iran and UAE over the war in the Middle East. Meanwhile, India’s position on the war is also delicate, with New Delhi balancing cordial relations with both Iran and Israel , but also being careful not to upset ties with Washington.

According to Kewalramani, the alliance will aim to address the war without naming countries.

“I would be surprised if they name the US and Israel. They will likely find a state of compromise and arrive at a statement on the war around the themes of sovereignty, territorial integrity of all countries and respecting legitimate interests and concerns,” he said.

Tensions between Iran and fellow BRICS member Saudi Arabia have similarly been brewing as Iran-backed Houthi forces in Yemen launch drones and missiles targeting energy facilities and other infrastructure in Saudi Arabia. Saudi Arabia also backs the internationally recognised government of Yemen that the Houthis are fighting, which lost control of the whole of Yemen’s Red Sea coast this week – including the strategically critical Bab al-Mandeb strait.

In July, Yemen government forces struck the international airport of Sanaa, which is held by the Houthis, to prevent aircraft they said were carrying Iranian weapons from landing.

Iran Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi spoke to his Saudi counterpart Faisal bin Farhan on Thursday night about “the escalation of tensions and the growing insecurity in the region”, according to Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

The ministry added that the two nations have “emphasised the need to continue cooperation and diplomatic efforts to prevent the spread of tensions and reestablish stability”.

Ties between the two Asian giants have been tense since a deadly military border clash in the Himalayas in 2020.

Relations have been warming recently, but deep mistrust remains over their contested frontier and a widening trade deficit, and their strategic rivalry still complicates ties.

Retired Colonel Bo said that China wants to position itself as the leading voice of the Global South at BRICS Summits. But he noted that some countries, including India, do not consider Beijing to be part of the Global South.

“A lot of other countries may say that China is now a global superpower,” he said. “China has, however, said that it is a natural member of the Global South. So China would place it firmly as a Global South country, as a developing country and talk about things from this perspective at the summit.”

Kewalramani said that while India and China will try to resolve their issues bilaterally, frictions over the purpose of BRICS will persist.

“Beijing looks at the BRICS as its premier institution to mobilise the Global South for its own interests, but also in terms of their shared grievances with regards to the West, particularly the US,” he said.

“India looks at the BRICS structurally as an entity that allows it to exercise strategic autonomy, build new partnerships, which is non-Western but not anti-Western,” he pointed out and added that this difference is not going to disappear at this summit.

“Russia and China are comfortable presenting BRICS as a counterweight to American and Western power, but India and several other members are much less interested in casting the organisation as an anti-Western alliance,” Reyes said.

Reyes said, however, the alliance is not meant to be like NATO or the EU where every member needs to agree on every geopolitical question for it to remain useful.

“The BRICS bring together countries that disagree with one another but share an interest in having greater room for manoeuvre internationally. It’s a group that bespeaks the idea of multipolarity as agency,” he said.

‘The real question is not whether the BRICS can achieve unity, which gets asked every time it meets. The better question is whether it can manage disagreement while still pursuing practical cooperation,” Reyes added.

As part of his unilateral foreign policy vision, Trump has both undermined the Western-led international order and lashed out at Global South blocs, such as BRICS, which he sees as a threat to the US’s economic dominance. He has called the grouping “anti-American”.

Retired Colonel Bo said that most Western leaders do not view Global South forums as anti-Western clubs. “But in the changing world order, which is reflected in multipolarity, they would watch these summits with great interest,” he added.

Reyes said Washington and the West should not be particularly concerned that BRICS is becoming a unified anti-US alliance or that its members will somehow engineer a toppling of the US dollar.

He noted that even Russia has said recently that it is not pursuing outright “de-dollarisation”. The members have different economic and strategic interests.

“What should matter to the US is why so many important countries want the BRICS to exist and expand. They want more choices. They want greater influence over global institutions. They want alternative financing and payment channels. And more and more, they want to insulate themselves from supply-chain disruption, sanctions, tariffs or political pressure emanating from any one major power,” he said.

He added that currently, those disruptions, coercions and stress are mainly coming from the US.

“So the deeper message for Washington is that, if the US treats every attempt at strategic autonomy as hostility, it may actually strengthen the forces driving countries towards the BRICS,” he said.

articles.title: Ukraine faces 'toughest winter' since Russia's full-scale invasion, UN warns
articles.summary: A senior UN official tells the BBC there is a race against the clock to ensure access to power and water through winter.
articles.body:
Ukraine is facing its "toughest winter" since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, a top United Nations official told the BBC.

Alexander De Croo, head of the UN development agency, said there was a risk of "humanitarian catastrophe" if Russian attacks cut off access to power and water.

Speaking in Ukraine, De Croo – the UN's third most senior official – accused Russia of systematically targeting the country's energy infrastructure. He said there was now a "race against the clock" to repair the power network before winter sets in and temperatures plummet.

Russia and Ukraine have been intensifying aerial attacks in recent months, and both deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure.

Russia's new jet-powered drones outpacing Ukraine's air defences with daily launches

Civilians told to flee Ukraine's fortress cities as Russia bids to control Donbas

Russia has started to use faster, jet-powered drones that are harder to intercept in recent around-the-clock attacks on Ukraine - and in particular Kyiv. Many of the strikes have targeted Ukraine's infrastructure, including businesses, warehouses, factories, petrol stations, as well as energy infrastructure.

Ukraine continues to launch drone strikes deep into Russian territory, largely against gas, oil and business distribution facilities. Both countries deny targeting civilians.

Deadly attacks have resumed after US President Donald Trump sent envoys for talks in Moscow with Russian President Vladimir Putin and in Kyiv with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky last weekend.

Five people were killed and 67 others were wounded in a daytime Russian drone strike on a shopping mall in Pavlohrad, a city in Dnipropetrovsk region, on Thursday, Ukrainian officials say. Earlier in the week two other shopping malls were targeted by Russian air strikes, killing two people and injuring 28 people in the attacks on the cities of Zaporizhzhia and Sumy.

Russia reported a Ukrainian seaborne drone attack on the resort city of Sochi overnight on Wednesday, in which 28 people were wounded, as well as three more deaths blamed on Ukrainian attacks.

Two people were also killed earlier this week when Russian drones hit a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, which has increasingly found itself caught up in the conflict.

A full-scale war has been raging between Russia and Ukraine since Putin launched an invasion more than four and a half years ago.

De Croo, a former prime minister of Belgium, told the BBC: "This winter is going to be the toughest one since the war".

He said Ukraine started "from a very weak base going into this winter". He added the UN were "very, very worried... about what this winter could become."

The concerns are driven by what De Croo said was Russia's "very systematic" targeting of civilian and energy infrastructure.

"This is petrol stations, it's shopping malls, it's business centres, but it's especially energy infrastructure, energy transmission lines, and so on. There is absolutely no justification for that," he said.

This could lead a "worst-case scenario" where people struggled to access energy to run heating, and water and sewage systems stopped working.

"With the temperatures that you would get here that would lead to circumstances which would be really close to humanitarian catastrophe," De Croo said.

Winter temperatures in Ukraine can drop to -20C.

If power supplies and critical infrastructure were severely damaged it could lead to "quite some human suffering", De Croo said.

Under efforts to prepare Ukraine for winter the UN Development Programme is helping to rebuild parts of its energy system that were damaged last winter. It is also establishing more sustainable and decentralised energy plants, which are less vulnerable to attack.

De Croo said completing the difficult and dangerous work was "almost an impossible task".

"They are reconstructing these sites under constant, constant air alarms. And they know that they are working at a site which is a target," he said. "So you try to reconstruct, but part of your day you can't work because it's just too dangerous."

articles.title: Ukraine is fighting Russia anywhere it can – even in the deserts of Africa
articles.summary: An elite group of Ukrainian drone operators has spent years hunting Russians from dugouts in Ukraine. They are now doing so in remote deserts thousands of miles from home.
articles.body: The conditions are grueling. Temperatures regularly soar above 110 degrees Fahrenheit during the day, then drop sharply overnight. Water is scarce and the dust and sand get everywhere. But at least they are working above ground. This elite group of Ukrainian drone operators has spent years hunting Russians from dugouts in Ukraine. They are still doing the same – but in the desert in northern Mali. Some 15 Ukrainian specialists have been deployed to the junta-led country in Africa’s Sahel region to assist local rebel forces who are fighting Russian troops – part of Kyiv’s mission to weaken its enemy wherever it operates. And Kyiv has also branched out to other theaters of conflict, capitalizing on its hard-won expertise in drone warfare to forge new anti-Russian partnerships. Speaking to Ukrainian soldiers and officers involved in operations in Mali and Libya, CNN can reveal for the first time the extent of these operations on other continents. A Ukrainian Defense Intelligence source with knowledge of the operations told CNN that several Ukrainian specialists were also stationed in Sudan and that troops from Chad, Niger and Burkina Faso had previously traveled to Mali to receive drone training from Ukrainian soldiers there. When Iran began striking US allies in the Middle East earlier this year, Ukraine sent teams of military experts to at least five countries in the Middle East. They spent several weeks teaching local forces how to take down the Iranian-made Shahed drones which Russia has been using to terrorize Ukraine for several years. One Ukrainian soldier who was deployed to the United Arab Emirates told CNN they were operating in combined teams with local troops driving alongside them and mirroring their every move. In exchange for sharing its know-how, Kyiv received an array of security cooperation agreements and promises of ammunition. In the Sahel, a vast semi-arid region to the south of the Sahara Desert, the situation is more complicated. Russia has been trying to assert itself as a power player in Africa, especially in the mineral-rich, coup-prone Sahel region. It has tried to fill the security void left by the withdrawal of French and other Western forces in recent years, propping up governments in exchange for cash and lucrative mining rights. At first, the Kremlin outsourced these operations to the Wagner Group, a private military company owned by entrepreneurial warlord Yevgeny Prigozhin. After Prigozhin’s death following his attempted coup in 2023, Moscow merged what remained of Wagner with its regular military, creating the Africa Corps, which deploys in support of Moscow’s local allies. ‘Serious adaptation’ The Ukrainian group in Mali is embedded with a separatist group that calls itself the Azawad Liberation Front and is composed mostly of northern Tuareg rebels. They are not directly involved in the frontline fighting but provide the rebels with support, training and operational help, two Ukrainians deployed there told CNN. “I coordinate their operations remotely. The signal from their drone comes to me over the internet, and I immediately tell them via radio what to do and where to fly,” one of the Ukrainian drone operators currently in Mali told CNN. “They go out on missions, then return to me, and we go over every detail of their actions. I don’t go out to the front lines myself — that was a direct order from my superiors,” he said. Russia has previously accused Ukraine of participating in massacres against civilians in Mali – an accusation Kyiv has denied. Separately, rights group Human Rights Watch released two reports over the summer accusing Russian troops in Mali of killing civilians, and another report that said that “all parties” directly engaged in the conflict unlawfully attacked civilians during a flare-up in violence in April. The report did not mention Ukraine. Asked about the allegations last month, Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told reporters the Africa Corps “operates strictly within the bounds of legality” and “in response to official requests from the legitimate governments of African states.” The Ukrainian Defense Intelligence source told CNN the point of the overseas deployments is to put pressure on Russia and undermine the notion that Moscow can be a reliable ally. “We are turning our experience in the field of (drones) into a foreign policy tool,” the source said. But he said the mission is also beneficial to the Ukrainians because it gives them a chance to test their equipment and skills in a completely different environment – and to show partners their methods work everywhere. “Dust and heat cause equipment to fail faster. Filters, cooling, electronics protection, batteries… everything works differently (and) requires serious adaptation,” he said, adding that even the way the war is fought is vastly different. “In Ukraine, it’s high intensity, massive strikes, constant pressure. Here it’s more of a maneuverable war over large territories, ambushes, route control, working in small groups and depending on knowledge of the terrain.” Differences in discipline and training require adaptation on both sides, he said, adding: “We teach them tactics; they teach us to survive and fight.” Russia is also using its operations in Africa to expand and adapt its military technology. Just this week, the state-owned weapons exporter, Rosoboronexport, presented new missiles and drones at the El Alamein International Airshow in Egypt, with the agency’s chief telling the Russian state news agency TASS these weapons are “proven” for combat in Africa and the Middle East. Growing confidence The Ukrainian contingents are small, but they are a sign of Ukraine’s growing confidence that its drone expertise has elevated its global status. Héni Nsaibia, West Africa senior analyst at Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED), an independent conflict monitor, told CNN that Mali is one of the countries where Russia now plays a crucial role. “They provide an essential lifeline to the regime,” he said, adding that Africa Corps forces have been “instrumental in preventing a more profound collapse, and possibly even the fall of the regime.” “But (the Russians) also need this military regime in place in order to be able to stay in Mali,” Nsaibia added. The first allegations that Ukraine was helping the Tuaregs came in 2024. In July that year, the rebels ambushed and killed dozens of Wagner fighters and Malian soldiers near the town of Tinzaouaten, on the border with Algeria. Andriy Yusov, the spokesperson for Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence, said at the time that the rebels received “necessary information” from Kyiv to fight the Russians. And while Ukraine later denied any substantial cooperation with the rebels, Yusov’s comment prompted a backlash from the military juntas of Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso, who lodged an official complaint with the United Nations Security Council, accusing Ukraine of sponsoring terrorists. CNN asked Defense Intelligence for comment for this article and was referred to earlier comments made by officials. The drone operator told CNN that Ukrainians also assisted rebels in the takeover of the strategic northern Mali town of Kidal earlier this year. The Tuareg rebels and militants linked to al Qaeda launched simultaneous attacks against the Russian troops, forcing them to withdraw. The Russian Defense Ministry accused Kyiv of playing a role in the attack, saying in a statement that “Ukrainian and European mercenary instructors” trained the rebels before the assault. Nsaibia said the Kidal takeover marked a key defeat for the Malian regime – and the Russian troops that have been propping it up. “It was a major setback that they lost Kidal and had to negotiate a safe corridor to be able to withdraw,” he told CNN. However, Nsaibia said that the situation could have been much worse for the Malian regime, had it not been for the assistance of Russia’s Africa Corps. ‘Attacked by the same idiots’ The attack in Kidal highlighted the massive difference drones can make on the battlefield in Mali and elsewhere in the Sahel, where war still tends to be fought in more traditional ways, using infantry troops equipped with rudimentary weapons. The Ukrainians in Mali told CNN the partnership with the Tuareg is one of convenience, not necessarily conviction. “Culture and religion are different, but when you are being attacked by the same idiots, ideological differences fade into the background,” the Defense Intelligence source said. The drone operator told CNN that his personal opinions and feelings are irrelevant. He described some of the rebels as “radicals” who are prone to spontaneously shoot in the air and act in “disruptive ways.” “Sometimes it’s emotionally hard to ignore certain things. It just so happens that we’re on the same side of the barricades right now… if these guys go on to successfully beat the Russians, we’ll be more than happy to train them,” he told CNN. He believes any operation that weakens the Russians can help Ukraine move the needle towards victory at home. “It puts pressure on them. This whole story has both psychological and real results,” he told CNN. A Russian ‘shadow’ fleet, and an escaped Ukrainian naval drone Earlier this year, a group of Greek fishermen spotted a mysterious black vessel floating near the country’s western island of Lefkada. It turned out to be a Ukrainian naval drone carrying explosives. Greece issued a formal diplomatic protest to Ukraine and Kyiv officially apologized for the incident, but it blamed Russia for creating the situation by attacking Ukraine and using a “shadow” fleet of oil tankers. These allow Russia to sell its oil in defiance of international sanctions, helping to finance the war. The drone had escaped from Ukrainian operators deployed to northwestern Libya, where they have been stationed since the end of 2025, the Ukrainian defense intelligence source told CNN. Their presence there was first reported by French public broadcaster RFI in the spring, and while never officially confirmed by the Ukrainian government, it is now an open secret. One Ukrainian naval drone operator deployed in Libya told CNN his unit was using the international military base in Misrata as a launchpad to attack Russia’s shadow fleet in exchange for training local forces. Like the aerial drone operator in Mali, he was recruited earlier this year by Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence straight from his previous post in Ukraine. Ukraine – a longstanding contributor to UN-peacekeeping missions in northern and central Africa before Russia’s full-scale invasion – has made no secret of its desire to become a different kind of player on the continent. Kyrylo Budanov, Ukraine’s former spy chief who is now the head of Zelensky’s presidential office, said in 2023 that Ukraine’s goal was to “keep killing Russians anywhere on the face of this world until the complete victory of Ukraine.” It’s a sentiment shared by all the Ukrainian troops who spoke with CNN. On Monday, Budanov once again pointed to Ukraine’s growing global footprint, posting a statement on social media celebrating its Defense Intelligence for protecting the country’s interests around the world, from “Russia to Africa, in a suit and in camouflage.”
