articles.title: Sunderland Culture House opens with library and arts space
articles.summary: The new hub in Sunderland is understood to have cost close to £4m.
articles.body:
A culture hub replacing a city's library and gallery spaces is to open later, months after it was supposed to and millions of pounds over budget.

Culture House Sunderland, near Keel Square in the city centre, is a multi-purpose venue featuring a library, exhibition and events spaces, bar and podcast studio.

Director Leanne Littlewood said "there's something for absolutely everybody across all of our spaces".

Originally billed to open in autumn 2025 at a cost of £27m, it is understood the final bill was closer to £40m because of increasing construction costs.

Littlewood said: "People can wander around, they can sit down and enjoy the space, they can take part in an activity that's happening on one of the many floors that we have."

The main atrium features moving screens for exhibitions and there is a green screen and cinema space, as well as a 360 degree immersion gallery.

"All of those spaces are centred around telling stories or creating connections or providing opportunities to the communities of Sunderland," Littlewood said.

The venue replaces Sunderland City Library, which has been closed since December, and will house the Northern Gallery for Contemporary Art - previously held in the now-closed The National Glass Centre.

articles.title: Africa world's most active terrorism theatre; reports more than two-thirds of ISIS activity: Report
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Africa has emerged as the world's most active theatre of terrorism, with more than two-thirds of Islamic State (ISIS) activity taking place on the con.
articles.body: Africa has emerged as the world's most active theatre of terrorism, with more than two-thirds of Islamic State (ISIS) activity taking place on the continent, according to a new report by the US House Committee on Homeland Security.The report, released in lieu of the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 attacks, said seven of the 10 countries with the highest number of terrorism-related deaths were in Africa, with five concentrated in the Sahel.It warned that the geographic shift in jihadist activity was creating new challenges for US counterterrorism efforts, with intelligence coverage and resources remaining uneven across the continent.The report, titled “25th Anniversary Report: National Security Improvements and the Domestic Threat Landscape 25 Years After 9/11/01,” assesses how the US security landscape has changed since the attacks and identifies emerging threats facing the country.“While terrorism has shifted geographically, it has also evolved operationally,” the committee said, pointing to the growing role of decentralised attacks and individuals radicalised without formal links to terrorist organisations.According to the report, more than two-thirds of ISIS's global activity during the first half of 2025 occurred in Africa, citing data from the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data project. It also cited the Global Terrorism Index, which found that ISIS and its affiliates were responsible for 1,805 deaths across 22 countries.The committee said the concentration of jihadist violence in Africa had exposed intelligence gaps and strained global counterterrorism resources.The shift is particularly significant because US counterterrorism policy has historically focused heavily on the Middle East, while the African theatre presents different challenges, including fragile governments, limited intelligence collection and uneven information-sharing capabilities.The report warned that extremist networks operating in Africa were increasingly using migration routes, smuggling networks and online platforms to extend their influence beyond the continent.The committee also said the nature of terrorism itself had changed since 9/11.Rather than relying exclusively on hierarchical organisations such as al-Qaida, extremist movements increasingly seek to inspire individuals to carry out attacks independently.The report said ISIS had encouraged supporters to launch attacks wherever they lived, reducing the need for direct command and control.It pointed to the January 2025 ISIS-inspired attack in New Orleans and the arrest of two US citizens the following month over an alleged ISIS-inspired plot in Michigan as examples of the changing threat.The number of radicalised young people with no formal affiliation to extremist organisations has also increased by more than 300% over the past decade, according to the report.Online propaganda, encrypted communications and social media have helped accelerate radicalisation while reducing the need for formal terrorist networks.The committee said this required a shift from an “organisation-centric” approach to counterterrorism towards prevention based on individual behaviour.The report also said the definition of the terrorist threat had widened considerably.The US has expanded its Foreign Terrorist Organisation framework to include violent cartels and other transnational criminal organisations, while also designating ideologically diverse extremist groups.The committee said this reflected a broader change in which terrorism, organised crime and foreign influence increasingly overlap.It cited Iran as an example of a state actor using criminal and terrorist proxies in overseas operations.The committee also warned that terrorism was increasingly intersecting with cyber capabilities.Terrorist organisations, criminal networks and hostile states are exploiting encrypted platforms, social media and emerging technologies including artificial intelligence, drones and 3D-printed weapons, it said.AI could help defenders analyse large amounts of security data and identify articles.title: Regulator says German gas storage may already be enough for winter
articles.summary: Germany's gas storage facilities should be sufficient to ensure supplies this winter despite comparatively low filling levels, the head of the Federal Networ...
articles.body:
Germany's gas storage facilities are currently at just over 55% of total capacity, with slightly more gas in storage than was withdrawn over the previous winter period.

Concerns have been raised about the low storage levels, leading to discussions about government-mandated purchases, which could be expensive.

Germany has LNG terminals along its coast that could provide additional supplies, with the possibility of importing more gas through these terminals to meet demand.

Germany's gas storage facilities should be sufficient to ensure supplies this winter despite comparatively low filling levels, the head of the Federal Network Agency has said.

Germany already had slightly more gas in storage than it withdrew over the entire previous winter period, Klaus Müller told dpa, adding that there was still time for further deposits in the coming weeks.

A little more than 136 terawatt hours of gas is currently stored, equivalent to just over 55% of total capacity. According to the regulator, just under 134 terawatt hours were withdrawn over the whole of last winter.

Storage levels are low compared with previous years, prompting concerns that the amount of gas currently stored may not be enough to last until spring.

The possibility of government-mandated purchases has also been discussed. While such measures are possible, they are likely to be expensive.

LNG terminals could provide additional supplies

Gas storage operators' association INES recently described the storage levels as "historically low" and called for rule changes to make storing gas financially worthwhile again.

However, comparisons with previous storage levels are complicated by the fact that Germany now has liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminals along its coast, allowing additional supplies to be imported relatively quickly from the global market.

Germany also continues to receive gas through pipelines, including from Norway.

Müller also pointed to the possibility of additional LNG imports.

"The LNG terminals currently have a utilization rate of around 45%. There is sufficient capacity to import additional gas," he said.

Like the German Economy Ministry, Müller currently sees no need for government intervention and is instead relying on the free market, he said.

articles.title: Brighton's art trail benches 'bring people together'
articles.summary: An art trail of "book benches" across Brighton and Hove is back for another year.
articles.body:
Thirty painted "book bench" sculptures have been placed across Brighton as part of a charity art trail.

The sculpture trail is designed as a walking route through the city from Saturday until 8 November.

As well as the painted book bench sculptures, schools and community groups have also designed an additional 40 mini book benches.

The trail will be raising money for Amaze, a Sussex charity which supports families with disabled children.

Hannah Allbrooke, head of fundraising and marketing at Amaze, said: "We've just installed one of the sculptures [at Jubilee Library] on the story trail, there's 74 book benches in total.

"After the sculptures are displayed, they go off to auction to raise money for us to help support families.

"It's really important to us that this was an accessible and fun experience. They can go out with families and enjoy a tactile, physical sculpture."

The art trail has been popular in previous years with Shaun the Sheep and snail sculptures dotted around the city .

Sarah Harvey, trail director for Wild in Art, said: "We work with charities across the UK, we feel they bring people together.

"There's so many people who bring this trail together, we have our artists but also businesses that sponsor the benches."

Artist Guy Parker-Rees, who designed the book bench at Jubilee Library, said: "I really enjoyed painting this bench, it's like a mini art gallery for everyone to explore. It's a great cause."

Jess Eyles, another artist, said: "This was my first time doing something like this.

"This was something that was a big adventure and out of my comfort zone."

articles.title: The slow, muddy work of saving the Isle of Man's ancient bogs
articles.summary: Sarah Hickey and her team help keep nearly 20,000 acres of upland in the Isle of Man healthy.
articles.body:
High up on a Manx hillside, Sarah Hickey effortlessly pushes a metre-long metal rod into the wet ground until it disappears almost to her hands.

"This is pretty deep here," she says, reading the markings on the probe. Beneath her boots is peat, built up over thousands of years and consisting of partially decayed plants and organic matter.

Hickey is the island's Peatland Officer and part of an Uplands team of just three, who, between them, manage about 8,000 hectares of the Island's hills.

Hickey's job is to find the parts of that landscape which have been damaged, and inject life into it.

Peat is partially decomposed vegetation that builds up in waterlogged ground over centuries, storing more carbon than any other soil on Earth.

"It's important to keep that carbon locked away and not released to the atmosphere," Hickey says.

Much of that carbon has stayed locked away, but not all of it. The island's uplands were largely stripped of trees by the 17th century, and with little timber left to burn, islanders turned to the hills for fuel instead.

Peat would be cut into blocks and left to dry; peat made a good, slow-burning fuel, and for generations it was what Manx households cooked on and heated their homes with.

The practice was banned in 2020, but the bare faces that cutting left behind are still collapsing and eroding today, washing sediment down into reservoirs.

Repairs start with a digger light enough not to cause fresh damage, which pulls the bare peat back to a gentler slope and folds the vegetation over it.

What is left exposed is protected with bio logs, then held down under netting, which keeps the ground shaded and damp so new vegetation can take hold.

The real engineer of a healthy bog, experts say though, is sphagnum moss.

"It grows in peatland habitats, but it also creates them," Hickey says.

It holds huge amounts of water, slowing rain as it moves downhill, reducing flooding and filtering out sediment before it reaches the reservoir.

It is also, she says, more fire-resistant; peat in good condition can be up to 90% water, which is increasingly important as wildfires become more common during summer months.

It matters for wildlife too. Ground-nesting birds such as hen harriers rely on open, treeless bog, safe from predators that would otherwise perch and watch for prey, while the wet ground breeds the invertebrates chicks are fed on.

The reward can arrive fast. After installing coir logs on one site last year, Hickey and colleagues sat down for tea beside the new pools they had created.

"Straight away there were dragonflies in that pool laying eggs," she says. "It was amazing to see what a difference these little features are making."
